126407.e: Higher luminosity means more collisions and therefore more data. This allows even very rare processes to be studied more precisely.
126407.m: The High-Luminosity LHC is meant to deliver many more collisions and data.

126408.q: How fast do the protons in the LHC move at full energy?
a: At over 99.9999 per cent of the speed of light
At about half the speed of light
At about 10 per cent of the speed of light
At about the speed of sound
126408.e: At energies in the TeV range, a proton’s total energy is thousands of times greater than its rest energy. Its speed is therefore extremely close to the speed of light, but never reaches it.
126408.m: In the LHC, the protons fly at almost the speed of light.

126409.q: Which fundamental force does the Standard Model of particle physics not describe?
126409.e: The Standard Model unites three of the four fundamental forces. Gravity is described by general relativity and has not yet been included in a quantum theory.
126409.m: Gravity is missing from the Standard Model.

126410.q: How many elementary matter particles (fermions, not counting antiparticles) does the Standard Model know?
126410.e: The Standard Model counts 12 elementary fermions. Each one also has an antiparticle.
126410.m: The Standard Model knows twelve elementary matter particles.

126411.q: Which particle carries the strong interaction?
126411.e: Gluons hold the quarks together in protons and neutrons. The name comes from the English word “glue”.
126411.m: Gluons glue the quarks together with the strong force.

126412.q: Which particle carries the electromagnetic interaction?
126412.e: Electrically charged particles interact by exchanging photons, the quanta of light.
126412.m: The photon carries the electromagnetic force.

126413.q: Which interaction do the W and Z bosons carry?
126413.e: The weak interaction is responsible, for example, for beta decay. Its exchange particles are very heavy, which is why it has an extremely short range.
126413.m: W and Z bosons carry the weak force.

126414.q: What did Glashow, Salam and Weinberg receive the Nobel Prize in Physics for in 1979?
a: For unifying the electromagnetic and weak interactions
126414.e: Their theory of the electroweak interaction describes two fundamental forces as forms of one common force.
126414.m: The electroweak theory unites two fundamental forces.

126415.q: What is the theory in the Standard Model that describes the strong interaction called?
126415.e: The name refers to “colour” (Greek chroma), a charge of the strong force.
126415.m: The strong force is described by quantum chromodynamics.

126416.q: To which group of particles do the force particles photon and gluon belong?
126416.e: Particles that carry forces have whole-number spin and are bosons. Matter particles such as electrons and quarks are fermions.

126417.q: How many kinds (flavours) of quarks are there in the Standard Model?
126417.e: The quarks are called up, down, charm, strange, top and bottom.
126417.m: There are six different kinds of quark.

126418.q: Which is the heaviest known quark?
126418.e: The top quark is about as heavy as a whole gold atom. It decays so quickly that it does not form bound particles.
126418.m: The top quark is the heaviest elementary particle.

126419.q: Where was the top quark discovered in 1995?
126419.e: The top quark was detected at Fermilab’s Tevatron accelerator near Chicago.
126419.m: The top quark was discovered at Fermilab in 1995.

126420.q: Which quarks make up a neutron?
a: Two down quarks and one up quark
Two up quarks and one down quark
One up, one down and one strange quark
126420.e: The neutron has the composition udd. The charges +2/3, −1/3 and −1/3 add up to zero.
126420.m: A neutron consists of one up quark and two down quarks.

126421.q: The delta particle Δ++ consists of three up quarks, each with +2/3 elementary charge. What charge does it have?
126421.e: You add the three charges: 3 times 2/3 gives 2. So the particle has the charge +2 e.
126421.m: The charge of a hadron is the sum of the quark charges.

a: Quarks never occur freely on their own
Quarks cannot move in atomic nuclei
Quarks can only exist in the laboratory
126422.e: The further apart quarks are pulled, the stronger the force between them becomes. Instead of single quarks, new quark-antiquark pairs are produced.
126422.m: Quarks always stay locked inside particles such as protons.

126423.q: From which literary work did Murray Gell-Mann borrow the word “quark”?
a: From “Alice in Wonderland” by Lewis Carroll
126423.e: “Finnegans Wake” contains the line “Three quarks for Muster Mark!”. The number three matched the three quarks in protons and neutrons.
126423.m: The name quark comes from a novel by James Joyce.

126424.q: What does a meson consist of?
126424.e: Mesons such as the pion consist of a quark-antiquark pair. Particles made of three quarks, by contrast, are called baryons.
126424.m: A meson consists of a quark and an antiquark.

126425.q: Which property of quarks is labelled with the names red, green and blue?
126425.e: Colour charge is the charge of the strong force. It has nothing to do with real colours; the names are just an image.
126425.m: Quarks carry a colour charge that has nothing to do with real colours.

126426.q: Which of these particles is a lepton?
126426.e: Leptons are elementary particles without quarks: the electron, muon, tau and the three neutrinos. The proton, pion and neutron are made of quarks.
126426.m: The muon is a heavy relative of the electron and a lepton.

126427.q: Which interaction do leptons not take part in?
a: None, they take part in all of them
126427.e: Leptons carry no colour charge and therefore do not feel the strong force. Charged leptons also interact electromagnetically.
126427.m: Leptons do not feel the strong force.

126428.q: Roughly how much heavier than an electron is a muon?
126428.e: The muon has about 207 times the mass of the electron but is otherwise very similar. It is unstable and decays after about two microseconds.
126428.m: The muon is about two hundred times heavier than the electron.

126429.q: Which charged lepton was the last to be discovered, in the mid-1970s?
126429.e: The tau was discovered in 1975 at SLAC in California by Martin Perl and his team. It is the heaviest charged lepton.
126429.m: The tau is the heaviest and most recently discovered charged lepton.

126430.q: What does the Greek word from which the term “lepton” comes mean?
126430.e: The word “leptos” means light or fine. The electron, as the first lepton, was much lighter than protons.

126431.q: Why do many muons from cosmic rays reach the ground even though they are very short-lived?
a: Because of time dilation at almost the speed of light
Because they are attracted by the Earth and speed up
Because they are newly formed near the ground
Because the atmosphere lengthens their lifetime
126431.e: For us, time passes more slowly in the fast muons. That is why they travel much longer distances than their lifetime at rest would allow.
126431.m: Muons from space demonstrate the time dilation of relativity.

126432.q: Where was the muon discovered in 1936?
a: In a particle accelerator at CERN
126432.e: Carl D. Anderson and Seth Neddermeyer found the muon in tracks of particles from cosmic rays. Accelerators of this power did not yet exist at the time.
126432.m: The muon was discovered in cosmic rays.

126433.q: Which quantity is conserved in all particle reactions observed so far, for example in the beta decay of a neutron?
a: The total mass of the particles
126433.e: In beta decay, an electron antineutrino is produced alongside the electron. The electron (+1) and antineutrino (−1) together give the lepton number zero, as before.
126433.m: In particle reactions, the lepton number is conserved.

126434.q: In which year did CERN announce the discovery of a Higgs boson?
126434.e: On 4 July 2012, the discovery of a new particle was presented that matches the long-sought Higgs boson.
126434.m: The Higgs boson was discovered in 2012.

126435.q: Roughly what mass does the Higgs boson have?
126435.e: At about 125 GeV, the Higgs boson is about 130 times as heavy as a proton.
126435.m: The Higgs boson has a mass of about 125 GeV.

126436.q: Who received the 2013 Nobel Prize in Physics for the theoretical prediction of the Higgs mechanism?
126436.e: Englert had published the idea in 1964 together with Robert Brout, and Higgs almost at the same time. Brout had died in 2011 and could no longer receive the prize.
126436.m: Higgs and Englert received the Nobel Prize for the Higgs mechanism.

126437.q: Why can’t a Higgs boson be seen directly in the detector?
a: It decays almost immediately into other particles
It is only produced outside the detector
126437.e: A Higgs boson only exists for a tiny fraction of a second. It is recognised by the particles it decays into, for example two photons.
126437.m: The Higgs boson is detected through its decay products.

126438.q: Which two LHC experiments jointly detected the Higgs boson?
126438.e: Two independent experiments with different detectors found the particle. That made the discovery particularly convincing.
126438.m: Two independent detectors confirmed the Higgs boson.

126439.q: What role does the Higgs field play in the Standard Model?
a: It gives elementary particles such as W bosons and quarks their mass
It determines the electric charge of particles
126439.e: Particles that interact strongly with the Higgs field are heavy, others are light. Photons do not interact with it and remain massless.
126439.m: Elementary particles get their mass from the Higgs field.

126440.q: Where does most of a proton’s mass come from?
a: From the binding energy of the strong interaction
From the quark masses produced by the Higgs field
From the electrons in the proton
126440.e: The three quarks make up only about one per cent of the proton’s mass. According to E = mc², the rest lies in the energy of the gluons and the motion of the quarks.
126440.m: The proton’s mass comes mainly from binding energy.

126441.q: Which decay of the Higgs boson was one of the most important discovery channels in 2012?
a: The decay into a single photon
The decay into a proton and an electron
The decay into a single neutrino
126441.e: Two high-energy photons can be measured very precisely in the detector. An excess at a certain mass revealed the new particle.
126441.m: The Higgs boson showed up, among other things, through decays into two photons.

126442.q: Which physicist predicted the existence of the positron with his relativistic equation for the electron?
126442.e: The Dirac equation of 1928 gave solutions that were interpreted as particles with positive charge and the electron’s mass.

126443.q: Who detected the positron in cosmic rays in 1932?
126443.e: In a cloud chamber inside a magnetic field, Anderson observed tracks that looked like electrons but curved in the opposite direction.
126443.m: The positron was discovered by Carl D. Anderson in 1932.

126444.q: What usually happens when an electron and a positron meet?
a: They combine to form a proton
126444.e: In annihilation, the entire mass is converted into radiation energy. Usually two gamma photons of 511 keV each are produced.
126444.m: Matter and antimatter annihilate each other into radiation.

126445.q: Where were antihydrogen atoms first produced in 1995?
126445.e: The first few antihydrogen atoms were produced in 1995 at CERN’s LEAR storage ring. Today CERN studies antimatter with the Antiproton Decelerator.
126445.m: The first anti-atoms were produced at CERN in 1995.

126446.q: Which medical imaging method uses positrons?
126446.e: In PET, the patient is given a weakly radioactive substance that emits positrons. The photons produced when these annihilate are measured.
126446.m: PET uses antimatter to make metabolic processes visible.

126447.q: What electric charge does an antiproton have?
126447.e: Antiparticles have the same mass but the opposite charge. The antiproton therefore carries the charge −1 e.
126447.m: Antiparticles have the opposite charge of their particle.

126448.q: How much energy is released when 1 g of antimatter annihilates completely with 1 g of matter, using c = 3 · 10^8 m/s?
126448.e: The entire mass of 2 g, so 0.002 kg, is converted. E = m · c² = 0.002 kg · 9 · 10^16 m²/s² = 1.8 · 10^14 J.
126448.m: In annihilation, the whole mass becomes energy according to Einstein’s formula.

126449.q: What did the ALPHA-g experiment at CERN show about antihydrogen in 2023?
a: It falls downwards in a gravitational field like normal matter
It rises upwards in a gravitational field
It is not affected by gravity at all
126449.e: The measurement confirmed that antimatter is attracted by gravity. This ruled out a repulsive “antigravity”.

126450.q: Which unsolved puzzle in physics concerns antimatter in the universe?
a: Why there is almost only matter and hardly any antimatter
Why antimatter is heavier than matter
Why antimatter only occurs on Earth
Why antimatter is slower than light
126450.e: In the Big Bang, matter and antimatter should really have been produced in equal amounts. Where the small excess of matter comes from has not yet been explained.
126450.m: Why the universe is made of matter is an open question.

126451.q: Where were neutrinos first detected directly in 1956?
126451.e: Clyde Cowan and Frederick Reines used the strong flow of neutrinos from a nuclear reactor in the USA. Reines later received the Nobel Prize for this.
126451.m: Neutrinos were first detected at a nuclear reactor in 1956.

126452.q: What does the observation of neutrino oscillations prove?
a: That neutrinos are faster than light
That there is only one kind of neutrino
126452.e: Neutrinos can change into another kind of neutrino along the way. This is only possible if they have a mass, even a tiny one. The Nobel Prize was awarded for this in 2015.
126452.m: Neutrino oscillations show that neutrinos have mass.

126453.q: Roughly how many neutrinos from the Sun hit one square centimetre of the Earth’s surface every second?
126453.e: Nuclear fusion in the Sun produces huge numbers of neutrinos. They pass through us all the time without us noticing anything.
126453.m: Every second, billions of solar neutrinos fly through our bodies.

126454.q: Where is the IceCube neutrino detector?
126454.e: IceCube uses a cubic kilometre of clear, deep Antarctic ice as a detector for high-energy neutrinos.
126454.m: The IceCube detector is buried in the ice of the South Pole.

126455.q: Which medium does the Super-Kamiokande detector in Japan use to detect neutrinos via Cherenkov light?
126455.e: A huge tank of ultra-pure water is surrounded by thousands of light sensors. Charged particles from neutrino reactions produce faint flashes of light in it.
126455.m: Super-Kamiokande looks for neutrinos in a huge water tank.

126456.q: What explained the apparently faster-than-light neutrinos sent from CERN to Gran Sasso in 2011?
a: A measuring error, partly caused by a badly fitted optical fibre connector
A mistake in the theory of relativity
126456.e: The OPERA experiment at first measured a flight time that was too short. Later, technical faults were found, and the neutrinos were not faster than light.
126456.m: Neutrinos are not faster than light either.

126457.q: Why do neutrinos pass through the whole Earth almost unhindered?
a: They are electrically neutral and only interact weakly
They are repelled by the Earth
They move more slowly than atoms
126457.e: Neutrinos feel neither the strong nor the electromagnetic force. That is why they react with matter only extremely rarely.
126457.m: Neutrinos hardly react with matter and fly straight through the Earth.

126458.q: During which event in 1987 were neutrinos from an exploding star measured for the first time?
a: During a meteorite impact in Siberia
During the flyby of Halley’s Comet
126458.e: The supernova in the Large Magellanic Cloud sent out a burst of neutrinos that was recorded by detectors in Japan and the USA.
126458.m: Supernova 1987A provided the first neutrinos from an exploding star.

126459.q: A proton passes through a voltage of 2000 V. How much kinetic energy does it gain?
126459.e: A particle with one elementary charge gains 1 eV per volt. At 2000 V, that is 2000 eV or 2 keV.
126459.m: One electronvolt is the energy of one elementary charge after one volt.

126460.q: Which former household appliance contained a small particle accelerator?
126460.e: In the picture tube, electrons were accelerated by a high voltage of several thousand volts and steered across the screen with magnetic fields.
126460.m: Old tube televisions were small electron accelerators.

126461.q: Who invented the cyclotron in the 1930s?
126461.e: In a cyclotron, particles spiral outwards in a magnetic field and are accelerated on each lap by an alternating electric field.
126461.m: Ernest Lawrence built the first cyclotron.

126462.q: Why are circular accelerators poorly suited for bringing electrons to the very highest energies?
a: On circular paths, electrons lose a lot of energy as synchrotron radiation
Electrons cannot be deflected by magnets
Electrons are too heavy for circular paths
126462.e: The radiation losses grow sharply with energy and are especially large for light particles. That is why linear accelerators tend to be used for very high electron energies.
126462.m: In a circular accelerator, light particles lose a lot of energy through radiation.

126463.q: Which facility at the Paul Scherrer Institute produces intense X-ray light with electrons on a circular path?
126463.e: The SLS is a synchrotron light source. The synchrotron radiation it deliberately produces is used, for example, to study materials and proteins.
126463.m: The Swiss Light Source uses synchrotron radiation for research.

126464.q: How are charged particles brought to higher energy in modern accelerators?
a: With electric fields in radio-frequency cavities
126464.e: Only electric fields can increase the energy of charged particles. Magnetic fields only change the direction of motion.
126464.m: Particles are accelerated by electric fields.

126465.q: What does the Paul Scherrer Institute also use accelerated protons for in medicine?
126465.e: Protons release their energy mainly at the end of their path. This allows tumours to be irradiated precisely while sparing the surrounding tissue.
126465.m: Protons can be used to irradiate tumours very precisely.

126466.q: Roughly what circumference is the Future Circular Collider (FCC) planned at CERN meant to have?
126466.e: The FCC would be more than three times as long as the LHC tunnel and would run under the Geneva area and France. No decision has yet been made on building it.
126466.m: The planned Future Circular Collider would be over three times as large as the LHC.

126467.q: At which research facility is the ATLAS particle detector?
a: At CERN’s Large Hadron Collider near Geneva
At the Paul Scherrer Institute in Villigen
126467.e: ATLAS is one of the large detectors at the LHC, CERN’s particle accelerator on the border between Switzerland and France. It records the collisions of protons.
126467.m: ATLAS is a detector at CERN’s LHC.

126468.q: Roughly how large is the ATLAS detector?
a: About 46 metres long and 25 metres high
About 4 metres long and 2 metres high
About 460 metres long and 250 metres high
About 15 metres long and 10 metres high
126468.e: ATLAS is about as tall as an eight-storey building and is considered the particle detector with the largest volume.
126468.m: ATLAS is the particle detector with the largest volume.

126469.q: Which long-sought particle did the ATLAS and CMS detectors detect in 2012?
126469.e: In 2012, ATLAS and CMS announced the discovery of the Higgs boson. It explains how elementary particles get their mass. The graviton has still not been detected.
126469.m: ATLAS and CMS discovered the Higgs boson in 2012.

126470.q: Why does the muon spectrometer form the outermost layer of ATLAS?
a: Because muons pass through the inner layers almost unhindered
Because muons are only produced outside the beam pipe
126470.e: Most other particles are stopped in the calorimeters. Muons get further and are therefore measured on the outside.
126470.m: Muons fly through almost everything, so they are measured right at the outside.

126471.q: What is the job of the calorimeters in the ATLAS detector?
a: To measure the energy of particles by stopping them
126471.e: In the calorimeters, particles produce showers whose total energy is measured. There are calorimeters for electrons and photons and for hadrons.
126471.m: Calorimeters measure the energy of particles.

126472.q: What is the ATLAS trigger system for?
a: It selects the interesting collisions to store in real time
It counts the visitors in the detector
126472.e: Far too many collisions take place every second to store them all. The trigger keeps only a small fraction of promising events.
126472.m: The trigger decides in a flash which collisions are stored.

126473.q: How does ATLAS detect particles such as neutrinos that leave the detector unnoticed?
a: Through missing momentum at right angles to the beam direction
Through their tracks in the inner detector
Through flashes of light in the magnets
126473.e: Before the collision, the particles have no total momentum at right angles to the beam. If momentum in this direction is missing afterwards, an invisible particle must have carried it away.
126473.m: Invisible particles give themselves away through missing momentum.

126474.q: How does the ATLAS inner detector measure the momentum of charged particles?
a: Through the curvature of their tracks in the magnetic field
Through the colour of their light
Through the sound of the impact
126474.e: A magnetic field bends charged particles onto curved paths. The greater their momentum, the weaker the curvature.
126474.m: The less a track is curved, the greater the particle’s momentum.

126475.q: What was the name of the first web browser, which Tim Berners-Lee programmed at CERN in 1990?
126475.e: The first browser was also an editor with which web pages could be edited. To avoid confusion with the web itself, it was later renamed Nexus.
126475.m: The first web browser was called WorldWideWeb.

126476.q: In which year did Tim Berners-Lee submit his first proposal for a networked information system at CERN?
126476.e: In March 1989 he wrote “Information Management: A Proposal”. His supervisor wrote “vague but exciting” on it.
126476.m: The World Wide Web began in 1989 with a proposal at CERN.

126477.q: Which Belgian computer scientist worked closely with Tim Berners-Lee at CERN on developing the web?
126477.e: In 1990, Robert Cailliau revised the project proposal with Berners-Lee and promoted the web at CERN.
126477.m: Robert Cailliau helped Tim Berners-Lee build the web.

126478.q: On which type of computer did the first web server at CERN run?
126478.e: Berners-Lee used a NeXT workstation. A note stuck on the machine said that it should not be switched off.
126478.m: The first web server ran on a NeXT computer at CERN.

126479.q: At which address could the world’s first website be reached?
126479.e: The page explained the World Wide Web project itself. CERN later restored it at the old address.
126479.m: The world’s first website was info.cern.ch.

126480.q: What did CERN decide about the World Wide Web in 1993?
a: To release the software to everyone without licence fees
To sell the web to a company
To allow the web only for physicists
126480.e: Because the web was free to use, companies and private individuals could use it at no cost. This contributed greatly to how quickly it spread.
126480.m: In 1993, CERN made the web available to everyone free of charge.

126481.q: What was the World Wide Web originally developed for at CERN?
126481.e: Thousands of researchers from all over the world worked with different computers. The web was meant to make documents easily accessible through hyperlinks.
126481.m: The web was meant to help researchers share information.

126482.q: Which markup language for web pages did Tim Berners-Lee develop at CERN?
126482.e: Hypertext Markup Language is used to describe the structure of web pages and set links. He also developed the transfer protocol HTTP and web addresses (URLs).
126482.m: Web pages are described with the language HTML.

126483.q: Which Swiss astronomer concluded in 1933 from observations of the Coma galaxy cluster that there must be invisible “dark matter”?
126483.e: Zwicky found that the galaxies in the cluster move too fast to be held together by the visible mass alone.
126483.m: Fritz Zwicky coined the term dark matter in 1933.

126484.q: According to current measurements, roughly what share of the total energy content of the universe does dark matter make up?
126484.e: According to measurements of the cosmic background radiation, the universe consists mostly of dark energy and dark matter. Dark matter contributes a good quarter.
126484.m: Dark matter makes up about a quarter of the universe.

126485.q: Roughly how many times more dark matter than ordinary matter is there in the universe?
126485.e: The measurements give a ratio of about five to one. So stars, gas, planets and we ourselves are only a small part of the matter.
126485.m: There is about five times more dark matter than ordinary matter.

126486.q: Which observation by Vera Rubin in the 1970s supported the existence of dark matter?
a: The measurement of the cosmic background radiation
126486.e: Stars at the edge of galaxies orbit almost as fast as those further in. This can only be explained by extra, invisible mass.
126486.m: Fast-orbiting stars at the edge of galaxies reveal dark matter.

126487.q: Which effect can be used to map the distribution of dark matter?
126487.e: Mass curves space and bends the light of galaxies behind it. From the distortions, the mass can be worked out even if it is invisible.
126487.m: Gravitational lenses make invisible mass visible.

126488.q: What does the abbreviation WIMP, a possible candidate for dark matter, stand for?
126488.e: WIMPs would be heavy particles that interact only weakly with ordinary matter. Despite sensitive detectors, none have been found so far.
126488.m: WIMPs are hypothetical heavy particles of dark matter.

a: Because it does not emit, absorb or reflect light
Because it only appears at night
Because it only occurs in black holes
126489.e: Dark matter only reveals itself through its gravity. As far as we know today, it does not interact with electromagnetic radiation.
126489.m: Dark matter is invisible and only shows itself through gravity.

126490.q: Which ESA space telescope, launched in 2023, is meant to map the distribution of dark matter and dark energy?
126490.e: Euclid observes billions of galaxies and measures their shapes and distances. From this, the distribution of dark matter in the cosmos can be reconstructed.
126490.m: The ESA telescope Euclid explores the dark universe.

126491.q: In which city did the naturalist Conrad Gessner work as town physician in the 16th century?
126491.e: Conrad Gessner was town physician of Zurich and also taught natural history there. He is one of the most important all-round scholars of the Swiss Renaissance.
126491.m: Conrad Gessner was town physician in Zurich.

126492.q: Which work by Conrad Gessner in several volumes is considered the foundation of modern zoology?
126492.e: In the “Historia animalium”, Gessner brought together the knowledge of his time about animals and added his own observations and woodcuts. The work appeared in several volumes from 1551.
126492.m: Gessner’s animal book “Historia animalium” founded modern zoology.

a: An atlas of the Alpine passes
126493.e: In it, Gessner listed thousands of works in Latin, Greek and Hebrew with their authors and contents. That is why he is considered the father of bibliography.
126493.m: With the “Bibliotheca universalis”, Gessner became the father of bibliography.

126494.q: Which parts of plants did Conrad Gessner consider especially important for classifying plants?
126494.e: Gessner realised early on that flowers, fruits and seeds show related plants better than leaf shape or usefulness. This idea later became the basis of botanical classification.
126494.m: Gessner recognised the value of flowers and fruits for classifying plants.

126495.q: Which mountain near Lucerne did Conrad Gessner climb in 1555 and describe in a separate text?
126495.e: In 1555 Gessner climbed Pilatus and described the climb and the plant life. He is therefore seen as an early example of someone climbing mountains for the joy of nature.

126496.q: Which epidemic disease did Conrad Gessner die of in Zurich in 1565?
126496.e: As town physician, Gessner cared for the sick during a wave of plague and caught it himself. He died in 1565 at the age of 49.
126496.m: Conrad Gessner died of the plague in 1565.

126497.q: Which plant family, which also includes the African violet, is named after Conrad Gessner?
126497.e: The genus Gesneria, and with it the gesneriad family (Gesneriaceae), honours Conrad Gessner. Many of its species grow in the tropics.
126497.m: The gesneriad family bears the name of Conrad Gessner.

126498.q: On which banknote of the sixth Swiss banknote series (from 1976) was Conrad Gessner shown?
126498.e: The National Bank’s sixth banknote series showed well-known figures from science and culture. Gessner appeared on the 50-franc note.
126498.m: Conrad Gessner was shown on the former 50-franc note.

126499.q: Which ornamental plant did Conrad Gessner describe in 1559, from a specimen in a garden in Augsburg, as one of the first people in central Europe?
126499.e: In 1559 Gessner saw a flowering tulip in Augsburg and described and drew it. That is why the garden tulip bears the name Tulipa gesneriana.
126499.m: Gessner was one of the first to describe the tulip in central Europe.

126500.q: What is the name of the main work of the Basel botanist Caspar Bauhin from 1623?
126500.e: The “Pinax theatri botanici” matched up the plant names used by earlier authors. For more than a century it was the most important reference work in botany.
126500.m: Caspar Bauhin’s “Pinax” was a great index of plant names.

126501.q: In which language did Caspar Bauhin write his “Pinax”?
126501.e: Around 1600, Latin was the common language of scholars in Europe. That way botanists from many countries could use the work.

126502.q: Which innovation in naming did Caspar Bauhin anticipate, which Carl Linnaeus later made the rule?
126502.e: Bauhin already named many plants with a genus name and a short extra word. In 1753, Linnaeus made this binomial nomenclature the binding rule.
126502.m: Bauhin anticipated Linnaeus’s two-part plant names.

126503.q: Which structure in the human body bears the name of Caspar Bauhin?
a: The valve between the small and large intestine
The valve between atrium and ventricle
The muscle at the entrance to the stomach
126503.e: Bauhin’s valve (the ileocaecal valve) lies where the small intestine joins the large intestine. Bauhin was not only a botanist but also an anatomist.
126503.m: Bauhin’s valve separates the small and large intestine.

126504.q: At which university did Caspar Bauhin teach anatomy and botany?
126504.e: Bauhin was a professor at the University of Basel, then the only university in the Swiss Confederation. He also laid out one of the first botanical gardens there.
126504.m: Caspar Bauhin taught at the University of Basel.

126505.q: What was the name of Caspar Bauhin’s older brother, who was also an important botanist?
126505.e: Johann Bauhin worked on a comprehensive history of plants, which only appeared after his death. Both brothers shaped botany around 1600.
126505.m: Johann and Caspar Bauhin were both botanists.

126506.q: Which plant genus with two-lobed leaves honours the Bauhin brothers?
126506.e: The two joined halves of a Bauhinia leaf are a reminder of the pair of brothers. Linnaeus explicitly explained the name with this leaf shape.
126506.m: The two-lobed leaves of Bauhinia recall the Bauhin brothers.

126507.q: Why had Caspar Bauhin’s family come to Basel?
a: As traders in the salt business
126507.e: His father, a doctor, had fled from France as a follower of the Reformation. Basel offered protection to many religious refugees.
126507.m: The Bauhin family came to Basel as religious refugees.

126508.q: Which poem by Albrecht von Haller from 1729 shaped the image of the mountains in the 18th century?
126508.e: In “Die Alpen” (The Alps), Haller praised the simple life of the mountain people and the beauty of mountain nature. The poem made the Alps known across Europe as a place people longed for.
126508.m: Haller’s poem “The Alps” made the mountains famous.

126509.q: At which German university did Albrecht von Haller teach anatomy, surgery and botany from 1736?
126509.e: In 1736 Haller was appointed to the newly founded University of Göttingen and stayed there for 17 years. He built up anatomy and botany there.
126509.m: Albrecht von Haller taught in Göttingen for a long time.

126510.q: Which distinction did Albrecht von Haller introduce into physiology?
a: Irritability of muscles and sensitivity of nerves
126510.e: In experiments, Haller showed that muscle fibres react to stimuli by contracting (irritability), while nerves carry sensation (sensibility). He is considered the founder of experimental physiology.
126510.m: Haller distinguished between irritability and sensibility.

126511.q: Why is Albrecht von Haller also considered an important botanist?
a: He described the plants of Switzerland in a comprehensive flora
He introduced the two-part Latin names for species
He bred the first potato varieties in Switzerland
126511.e: In 1768 Haller published a large flora of Switzerland’s native plants with thousands of precisely described species. The two-part Latin names, on the other hand, go back to Carl Linnaeus.
126511.m: Haller wrote a comprehensive flora of Switzerland.

126512.q: On which banknote of the sixth Swiss banknote series (from 1976) was Albrecht von Haller shown?
126512.e: The National Bank’s sixth banknote series honoured figures from science and the arts. Haller appeared on the 500-franc note.
126512.m: Albrecht von Haller was on the former 500-franc note.

126513.q: For which journal did Albrecht von Haller write thousands of book reviews?
126513.e: Haller ran the “Göttingische Gelehrte Anzeigen” and wrote a huge number of reviews himself. In this way he followed the science of the whole of Europe.
126513.m: Haller wrote thousands of reviews for the “Göttingische Gelehrte Anzeigen”.

126514.q: Which position did Albrecht von Haller hold from 1758 in Roche in Vaud?
126514.e: Bern appointed Haller director of the salt works in Roche. During this time he also studied the plants of Vaud and Valais.
126514.m: Haller ran the salt works of Roche.

126515.q: In which city was Albrecht von Haller born in 1708 and where did he die in 1777?
126515.e: Haller came from a Bernese patrician family and returned to his home town in 1753. He died there in 1777.
126515.m: Albrecht von Haller was from Bern.

126516.q: Which famous doctor did Albrecht von Haller study under in Leiden?
126516.e: Boerhaave was the most influential teacher of medicine in Europe in his time. Haller completed his medical studies in Leiden.
126516.m: Haller studied under Herman Boerhaave in Leiden.

126517.q: Which technical term did Augustin-Pyramus de Candolle coin in 1813?
126517.e: In his “Théorie élémentaire de la botanique”, Candolle called the study of classifying living things “taxonomy”. The word comes from the Greek taxis (order) and nomos (law).

126518.q: What was the aim of the work “Prodromus systematis naturalis regni vegetabilis”, begun by Augustin-Pyramus de Candolle?
a: To describe all known seed plants
To illustrate all the fungi of Europe
To sort medicinal plants by their effects
126518.e: The “Prodromus” was meant to describe all known seed plants systematically. After Candolle’s death, his son Alphonse continued the work.
126518.m: The “Prodromus” aimed to cover all seed plants.

126519.q: Which institution in Geneva goes back to Augustin-Pyramus de Candolle?
126519.e: In 1817 Candolle founded Geneva’s first botanical garden in the Parc des Bastions. Today’s Conservatoire et Jardin botaniques grew out of it.
126519.m: Candolle founded the Geneva Botanical Garden.

126520.q: With which naturalist, who put forward an early theory of evolution, did Candolle publish the “Flore française”?
126520.e: Even before Darwin, Lamarck argued that species change. He had started the “Flore française”, and Candolle revised it heavily in 1805.
126520.m: Candolle worked on the “Flore française” together with Lamarck.

126521.q: In which country was Augustin-Pyramus de Candolle a professor before he returned to Geneva in 1816?
126521.e: Candolle was professor of botany in Montpellier in southern France. After that he worked in Geneva until his death.

126522.q: What did Augustin-Pyramus de Candolle show when he kept mimosa plants under constant light?
a: Their leaves follow an inner rhythm
Their leaves stay closed all the time
Their leaves grow twice as fast
126522.e: The leaves kept opening and closing, with a rhythm of a little less than 24 hours. This was an early sign of an inner clock in plants.
126522.m: Candolle found a sign of plants’ inner clock.

126523.q: Which idea of Augustin-Pyramus de Candolle did Charles Darwin later take up?
a: Species are created one by one
126523.e: Candolle said that all the plants in one place are at war with each other. Darwin took this picture of competition for his theory of selection.
126523.m: Candolle described the competition between plants.

126524.q: What did Alphonse de Candolle, the son of Augustin-Pyramus de Candolle, present in 1867?
a: A map of the Swiss mires
126524.e: Alphonse de Candolle drew up laws of botanical nomenclature, which an international congress adopted. They are a forerunner of today’s code for plant names.
126524.m: Alphonse de Candolle created early rules for plant names.

126525.q: In which city was Augustin-Pyramus de Candolle born in 1778?
126525.e: Candolle came from a Geneva family with roots in Provence. Geneva was still an independent republic at the time.
126525.m: Augustin-Pyramus de Candolle was from Geneva.

126526.q: What did Simon Schwendener discover around 1867 about the structure of lichens?
a: They consist of a fungus and an alga
126526.e: Schwendener showed that lichens are a partnership between a fungus and an alga. Today such partnerships are called symbiosis.
126526.m: Schwendener discovered the dual nature of lichens.

126527.q: Which canton did the botanist Simon Schwendener come from?
126527.e: Schwendener was born in 1829 in Buchs in the St Gallen Rhine Valley. He became one of the best-known plant anatomists of his time.
126527.m: Simon Schwendener came from Buchs SG.

126528.q: At which university did Simon Schwendener teach from 1878 until old age?
126528.e: After Basel and Tübingen, Schwendener was appointed to Berlin. There he ran the Botanical Institute for more than three decades.
126528.m: Schwendener taught in Berlin for decades.

126529.q: Which comparison did Simon Schwendener make in his work on the mechanical principle in the structure of plants?
a: Supporting tissues are like girders in building
Vascular bundles are like electric cables
126529.e: Schwendener showed that supporting tissues in stems are arranged the way an engineer would arrange girders. With this he founded technical plant mechanics.
126529.m: Schwendener compared plant stems with engineering structures.

126530.q: Which topic did Simon Schwendener deal with in his “Mechanical Theory of Leaf Arrangement”?
a: The arrangement of leaves on the shoot
The colouring of leaves in autumn
126530.e: Leaf arrangement (phyllotaxis) often follows regular patterns. Schwendener explained it with the pressure that young leaf buds put on each other.

126531.q: Which instrument was essential for Simon Schwendener’s studies of the structure of lichens around 1867?
126531.e: Schwendener studied the fine structures of lichens under the light microscope. He even wrote a textbook about the microscope together with Carl Wilhelm von Nägeli. The electron microscope only existed from the 1930s.
126531.m: Schwendener studied plants with the light microscope.

126532.q: How did many lichen researchers first react to Simon Schwendener’s explanation of lichens?
a: They thought it was already known
They ignored lichens from then on
126532.e: Many lichenologists saw lichens as independent organisms and fought the theory for a long time. Only later did Schwendener’s view win through.
126532.m: Schwendener’s lichen theory met with resistance at first.

126533.q: Which cells of the stomata did Simon Schwendener study for their mechanics?
126533.e: Two guard cells surround each stoma and open or close it through changes in pressure. Schwendener explained this movement by the structure of their cell walls.
126533.m: Guard cells open and close the stoma.

126534.q: At which university did Carl Schröter teach botany for decades?
126534.e: Schröter was professor of special botany at the Federal Polytechnic, today’s ETH Zurich. He shaped generations of Swiss botanists.
126534.m: Carl Schröter taught at ETH Zurich.

126535.q: What is the title of Carl Schröter’s great work on mountain vegetation?
126535.e: In “Das Pflanzenleben der Alpen” (Plant Life of the Alps), Schröter described the structure, way of life and adaptations of Alpine plants. The book became a standard work of Alpine botany.
126535.m: Schröter described the plant life of the Alps.

126536.q: Carl Schröter played a major part in founding which institution in 1914?
126536.e: Together with other naturalists, Schröter campaigned for a protected area in the Lower Engadine. In 1914 the first national park in the Alps was created there.
126536.m: Carl Schröter helped to found the National Park.

126537.q: Which two ecological terms go back to Carl Schröter?
126537.e: Autecology studies a single species and its environment, synecology whole communities. Schröter introduced this distinction around 1900.
126537.m: Schröter distinguished between autecology and synecology.

126538.q: What did Carl Schröter study together with Friedrich Gottlieb Stebler?
126538.e: Stebler and Schröter studied the plants of Swiss meadows and their value as fodder. This led to a well-known work on the best forage plants.
126538.m: Schröter and Stebler studied the forage plants of meadows.

126539.q: When was the botanist Carl Schröter mainly active?
126539.e: Carl Schröter lived from 1855 to 1939. His most important works and the founding of the National Park date from around 1900.

126540.q: Which handy identification book for mountain hikers did Carl Schröter publish?
126540.e: The “Taschenflora des Alpen-Wanderers” (Pocket Flora of the Alpine Hiker) showed common Alpine plants in coloured pictures. It appeared in many editions.
126540.m: Schröter’s pocket flora helped hikers identify plants.

126541.q: Which basic work on wetlands did Carl Schröter write in 1904 with the geographer Jakob Früh?
126541.e: In “Die Moore der Schweiz”, Früh and Schröter described the formation, plant life and distribution of Swiss mires. The work is still an important source today.
126541.m: Früh and Schröter described the mires of Switzerland.

126542.q: In which town was the plant sociologist Josias Braun-Blanquet born in 1884?
126542.e: Braun-Blanquet came from Chur and first studied the flora of the Grisons. Later he worked mainly in France.

126543.q: In which French university town did Josias Braun-Blanquet work for most of his life?
126543.e: Braun-Blanquet studied in Montpellier and stayed there. The city became a centre of plant sociology.
126543.m: Braun-Blanquet did most of his research in Montpellier.

126544.q: What is the title of the textbook Josias Braun-Blanquet published in 1928?
126544.e: The book, “Pflanzensoziologie” in German, set out the basics and methods of vegetation science. It appeared in several editions and translations.

126545.q: What does plant sociology, shaped by Josias Braun-Blanquet, study?
a: Which plant species occur together in communities
How people use plants in everyday life
126545.e: Plant sociology describes typical plant communities, such as a certain kind of beech forest or a nutrient-poor meadow. It classifies them by species that often grow together.
126545.m: Plant sociology studies communities of plants.

126546.q: In Josias Braun-Blanquet’s method, what are species called that are typical of a particular plant community?
126546.e: Character species occur mainly in one particular community. They are used to recognise the association.
126546.m: Character species show a particular plant community.

126547.q: Which regional flora did Josias Braun-Blanquet write together with Eduard Rübel?
126547.e: Braun-Blanquet and Rübel described the plant life of the Grisons in several volumes. Braun-Blanquet knew the canton well from his youth.
126547.m: Braun-Blanquet and Rübel wrote the flora of the Grisons.

126548.q: Using Josias Braun-Blanquet’s method, how do you record how strongly a plant species is represented on an area?
a: You estimate its cover in steps
You measure the height of the tallest tree
126548.e: Braun-Blanquet developed a scale for estimating the share of an area covered by a species. This makes it possible to compare many surveys quickly.
126548.m: In Braun-Blanquet’s method, the cover of each species is estimated.

126549.q: What is a vegetation survey (relevé) in Josias Braun-Blanquet’s sense?
a: A species list for a sample plot with estimated values
An aerial photo of a forest
A sound recording in the forest
126549.e: On a standard plot, you list all plant species and estimate their cover. Many such surveys are compared in tables.
126549.m: A vegetation survey records all species on a plot.

126550.q: Where does the second part of the name Braun-Blanquet come from?
126550.e: Josias Braun married Gabrielle Blanquet and afterwards used the double-barrelled name. She also supported him in his work.
126550.m: Braun-Blanquet included his wife’s name in his double-barrelled name.

126551.q: At which university was Albert Frey-Wyssling professor of plant physiology?
126551.e: Frey-Wyssling taught and did research at ETH Zurich for decades. He was one of the pioneers of cell biology.
126551.m: Albert Frey-Wyssling did research at ETH Zurich.

126552.q: Albert Frey-Wyssling was professor of plant physiology. What does this subject deal with?
126552.e: Plant physiology studies how plants grow, take up substances and gain energy. Frey-Wyssling taught this subject at ETH Zurich and was its rector from 1957 to 1961.
126552.m: Plant physiology studies the life processes of plants.

126553.q: Which field of research made Albert Frey-Wyssling known internationally?
a: Fine structure below the limit of the light microscope
126553.e: Frey-Wyssling studied the submicroscopic structure of cell walls and protoplasm. This made him a pioneer of research into ultrastructure.
126553.m: Frey-Wyssling studied the submicroscopic structure of cells.

126554.q: From which thread-like building blocks is the plant cell wall, which Albert Frey-Wyssling studied in detail, made?
126554.e: Long cellulose molecules join together into microfibrils, which are embedded in a matrix. Their direction determines how strong the cell wall is.
126554.m: The cell wall is built from cellulose microfibrils.

126555.q: With which instrument could Albert Frey-Wyssling see structures from the 1940s that are invisible in the light microscope?
126555.e: The electron microscope uses electron beams instead of light and therefore reaches a much higher resolution. Frey-Wyssling was one of the first botanists to use it.
126555.m: The electron microscope shows structures beyond the light microscope.

126556.q: Which light effect do ordered molecules such as cellulose show in a microscope with polarised light?
126556.e: Ordered molecular structures refract polarised light by different amounts depending on the direction. Albert Frey-Wyssling used this to work out the direction of the cellulose in cell walls.
126556.m: Birefringence in polarised light reveals ordered molecules.

126557.q: Which plant substance did Albert Frey-Wyssling study on Sumatra as a young man?
126557.e: Around 1930, Frey-Wyssling worked for a few years at a rubber research station in Medan on Sumatra. Then in 1932 he returned to ETH Zurich.

126558.q: What are Elias Landolt’s ecological indicator values used for?
a: To work out the site conditions from the plants growing there
To sort plants by their market value
To find out the age of trees
To assess how poisonous fungi are
126558.e: Each plant species gets numbers, for example for moisture, light and nutrients. From the species in a meadow you can then tell how wet or nutrient-rich the soil is. Heinz Ellenberg created similar values for central Europe.
126558.m: Indicator values reveal the properties of a site from the plants growing there.

126559.q: What does the moisture value in Elias Landolt’s indicator values show?
a: How moist the site of a species is
How much water the plant stores
How often it rains in a year
How high the water table is
126559.e: The moisture value describes the average soil moisture at a species’ typical site. If many species with high moisture values grow in one place, the soil is wet.
126559.m: The moisture value describes the soil moisture at the site.

126560.q: Many species with a high nutrient value according to Landolt grow in a meadow. What can you conclude from this?
a: The soil is rich in nutrients, for example from fertiliser
The soil is very acidic and poor
The meadow lies above the tree line
126560.e: The nutrient value describes how many nutrients, especially nitrogen, a species needs at its site. Many species with high values point to fertilised, rich meadows.
126560.m: High nutrient values show nutrient-rich soils.

126561.q: What does a high light value for a plant species mean in Elias Landolt’s indicator values?
a: It mainly grows in bright, open places
It mainly grows in deep forest shade
It needs artificial light in a greenhouse
126561.e: The light value shows how much light a species needs at its site. Species with a high light value grow in open meadows and on rocks, those with a low light value in shady forest.
126561.m: A high light value shows a light-loving species.

126562.q: Which city flora did Elias Landolt publish in 2001?
a: Flora of the City of Zurich
Flora of the City of Bern
Flora of the City of Basel
Flora of the City of Geneva
126562.e: Over many years, Landolt recorded the wild plants in the area of the city of Zurich. The work also documents changes since the 19th century.
126562.m: Landolt wrote the flora of the city of Zurich.

126563.q: Why do many Alpine plants, as described by Elias Landolt in “Our Alpine Flora”, grow as low cushions?
a: This protects them from wind and cold
This way they need less light
This way they are invisible to pollinators
126563.e: In flat, dense cushions it is warmer and less windy than in the surroundings. This way the plants lose less water and heat.
126563.m: Growing as cushions protects Alpine plants from wind and cold.

126564.q: Which institute did Elias Landolt run at ETH Zurich?
126564.e: Landolt was professor of geobotany and director of the Geobotanical Institute of ETH (Rübel Foundation). There, the distribution of plants and vegetation were studied.
126564.m: Landolt ran the Geobotanical Institute of ETH.

126565.q: What do botanists use the indicator values that Elias Landolt developed for the Swiss flora for?
a: To work out the site conditions from the plants
To find out the age of trees
To check how poisonous fungi are
126565.e: Indicator values show under which conditions a plant species typically grows, for example in terms of light, moisture or nutrients. From the species in a place you can then work out what the site is like.
126565.m: Indicator plants reveal the conditions where they grow.

126566.q: Which two universities run their plant collections together as the Zurich Herbaria?
a: University of Zurich and ETH Zurich
ETH Zurich and University of Bern
University of Zurich and University of Basel
126566.e: The herbaria of the University and of ETH Zurich have been combined as the United Herbaria. They are among the largest collections in Switzerland.
126566.m: The University and ETH Zurich share the Zurich Herbaria.

126568.q: Which details must a herbarium specimen definitely have?
a: Place found, date and name of the collector
Price and weight of the plant
126568.e: Without the place and date, a specimen is hardly any use for research. Only with these details can it show where and when a species occurred.
126568.m: A herbarium specimen needs the place found and the date.

126569.q: What do herbarium specimens collected over many decades show?
a: How the distribution and flowering time of plants have changed
How much money the plants cost
What the weather was like on the collecting day
126569.e: By comparing old and new specimens, you can see whether species have become rarer, spread to new areas or flower earlier. In this way herbaria also help to study climate change.
126569.m: Old herbarium specimens show changes in the plant world.

126570.q: Apart from identification, what do researchers use old herbarium specimens for today?
126570.e: DNA can often still be extracted from dried specimens. Collection data over decades also show how distribution and flowering times have changed.
126570.m: Old herbarium specimens also provide DNA for research.

126571.q: What is the herbarium specimen called on which the first description of a plant species is based and to which its name is tied?
126571.e: The holotype is the one specimen that the author chooses when first describing the species. Herbaria guard such type specimens especially carefully.
126571.m: The holotype anchors the name of a species.

126572.q: What is the rough number of specimens in the Zurich Herbaria?
126572.e: The Zurich Herbaria keep several million plant specimens from all over the world. That makes them one of the larger collections in Europe.
126572.m: The Zurich Herbaria hold millions of specimens.

126573.q: What were early herbaria with dried plants called in Latin?
126573.e: “Hortus siccus” means “dry garden”. In the 16th century, scholars began to keep pressed plants in books.

126574.q: How do herbaria today usually protect new or borrowed specimens from harmful insects?
126574.e: Specimens are frozen for a few days at very low temperatures, which kills insects and their eggs. In the past, poisonous substances were used for this.
126574.m: Deep-freezing protects herbarium specimens from insects.

126575.q: Above which place in the Bernese Oberland is the Schynige Platte Alpine Botanical Garden?
126575.e: The Schynige Platte lies south-east above Interlaken and high above Lake Brienz. From there the view stretches far into the Bernese Oberland.
126575.m: The Schynige Platte Alpine Garden lies above Interlaken.

126576.q: At roughly what altitude is the Schynige Platte Alpine Botanical Garden?
126576.e: The garden lies just under 2,000 metres above sea level. Typical plants of the subalpine and alpine zones grow well at this height.
126576.m: The Schynige Platte Alpine Garden is at about 2,000 metres.

126577.q: Which railway takes you to the Schynige Platte Alpine Botanical Garden?
126577.e: The Schynige Platte railway has been running up from Wilderswil since the 19th century. It is a cog railway with historic carriages.
126577.m: A cog railway runs from Wilderswil to the Schynige Platte.

126578.q: Which plants does the Schynige Platte Alpine Botanical Garden show?
a: Wild plants of the Swiss Alps
126578.e: The garden shows native Alpine plants in their natural communities. It is used for education and research.
126578.m: Wild plants of the Swiss Alps grow on the Schynige Platte.

126579.q: When is the Schynige Platte Alpine Botanical Garden open?
a: Only in the summer half of the year
126579.e: Because of snow, the garden can only be visited from about the end of May to the end of October. The mountain railway also only runs during this time.
126579.m: The Schynige Platte Alpine Garden only opens in summer.

126580.q: Which university looks after the Schynige Platte Alpine Botanical Garden scientifically?
126580.e: The garden works closely with the Institute of Plant Sciences and the Botanical Garden of the University of Bern. The university has held courses in Alpine botany there since 1932.
126580.m: The University of Bern looks after the Schynige Platte Alpine Garden.

126581.q: In which decade was the Schynige Platte Alpine Botanical Garden founded?
126581.e: The garden was set up in 1928 and opened to the public in 1929. It is one of the oldest Alpine gardens in Switzerland.
126581.m: The Schynige Platte Alpine Garden was created in the 1920s.

126582.q: Which famous group of mountains can you see from the Schynige Platte Alpine Botanical Garden?
126582.e: From the Schynige Platte there is a clear view of the famous trio of peaks of the Bernese Oberland. The view attracts many visitors.
126582.m: From the Schynige Platte you can see the Eiger, Mönch and Jungfrau.

126583.q: In which mountain village in Valais is the Jardin alpin Flore-Alpe?
126583.e: Flore-Alpe is in Champex-Lac in Lower Valais. The garden is a popular destination for plant lovers.
126583.m: The Jardin alpin Flore-Alpe is in Champex-Lac.

126584.q: At roughly what altitude is the Jardin alpin Flore-Alpe?
126584.e: The garden lies at about 1,500 metres above sea level. Many plants from higher up also grow well there.

126585.q: Why do many mountain plants grow well in the Jardin alpin Flore-Alpe?
a: It is itself in the mountains at about 1,500 m
126585.e: The garden is in Champex-Lac at about 1,500 metres above sea level. The cool mountain climate suits many plants from higher up.
126585.m: Alpine gardens are often in the mountains themselves.

126586.q: Apart from the pleasure of looking, what is an Alpine botanical garden such as Flore-Alpe for?
126586.e: Alpine gardens show and care for mountain plants from all over the world. They are also used for education, research and protecting rare species.
126586.m: Alpine gardens protect and show mountain plants.

126587.q: Where do the plants in the Jardin alpin Flore-Alpe come from?
a: From mountains all over the world
126587.e: As well as Alpine plants, the garden shows about 4,000 species, including some from mountains on other continents. This makes it possible to compare adaptations to similar habitats.
126587.m: Flore-Alpe shows mountain plants from all over the world.

126588.q: On which lake is the village with the Jardin alpin Flore-Alpe?
126588.e: The small mountain lake gave the village of Champex-Lac its name. The garden lies on the slope above the lake.
126588.m: Flore-Alpe is by the Lac de Champex.

126589.q: In which language region of Switzerland is the Jardin alpin Flore-Alpe?
126589.e: Champex-Lac is in French-speaking Lower Valais. That is why the garden has a French name.

126590.q: In what kind of design are the plants in the Jardin alpin Flore-Alpe mainly shown?
a: In rock gardens with rocks and streams
126590.e: Rocks, scree and streams imitate the natural habitats of mountain plants. This design is typical of Alpine gardens.
126590.m: Alpine gardens usually show plants in rock gardens.

126691.q: What is the main anatomical work that Andreas Vesalius published in 1543 called?
126691.e: The “Fabrica” of 1543 showed the human body in precise woodcuts. It is regarded as the beginning of modern anatomy.

126692.q: In which Swiss city was Vesalius's “Fabrica” printed?
126692.e: Vesalius had his work produced by the Basel printer Johannes Oporinus. At that time Basel was an important centre of book printing.
126692.m: The most important anatomy book of the Renaissance was printed in Basel.

126693.q: Whose teachings, an ancient doctor's, did Vesalius correct on many points?
126693.e: Galen's anatomy was considered untouchable for over a thousand years. Through his own dissections, Vesalius showed that it contained many errors.
126693.m: Vesalius questioned Galen's authority through his own observation.

126694.q: Why did Galen's anatomy contain errors that Vesalius uncovered?
a: Galen had not owned a magnifying glass
126694.e: In ancient Rome, dissecting humans was hardly possible. Galen therefore transferred findings from monkeys and pigs to humans.
126694.m: Galen's errors came from dissecting animals instead of humans.

126695.q: Which specimen prepared by Vesalius himself is still preserved in a Swiss museum today?
126695.e: During his stay in Switzerland in 1543, Vesalius prepared the skeleton of an executed man. It is considered one of the oldest surviving anatomical specimens.
126695.m: A skeleton prepared by Vesalius is still preserved in Switzerland.

126696.q: At which university did Vesalius teach anatomy and surgery as a young professor?
126696.e: Straight after gaining his doctorate, Vesalius became a professor in Padua in 1537. At that time the university was a leading centre of medicine.
126696.m: Vesalius taught in Padua, the centre of medicine at that time.

126697.q: What was new about the way Vesalius taught anatomy?
a: He only read aloud from old texts
He left everything to the students
126697.e: Before, the professor read aloud from Galen while an assistant dissected. Vesalius carried out the dissection himself and compared the text with the body directly.
126697.m: Vesalius made his own dissection the basis of teaching.

126698.q: Whose personal physician did Andreas Vesalius become?
126698.e: Vesalius entered the service of Emperor Charles V and later of his son Philip II of Spain.
126698.m: Vesalius served as personal physician at the court of Emperor Charles V.

126699.q: What did William Harvey describe in 1628 in his work “De motu cordis”?
126699.e: Harvey showed that the heart pumps the blood around the body in a closed circuit. This contradicted Galen's centuries-old teaching.
126699.m: Harvey discovered that blood circulates in the body.

126700.q: Which country did William Harvey come from?
126700.e: Harvey was an English doctor who worked in London after studying abroad.
126700.m: William Harvey was an English doctor.

126701.q: With which argument did Harvey disprove the idea that blood is constantly being newly made?
a: The heart pumps far too much blood for that
126701.e: Harvey estimated the amount pumped out with each heartbeat and multiplied it up. In a short time this came to more blood than a person could take in with food, so it must circulate.
126701.m: Harvey proved circulation with a simple calculation of quantities.

126702.q: According to Galen's teaching, which Harvey disproved, in which organ was blood made?
126702.e: Galen believed that the liver constantly made new blood from food, which was used up in the organs. Harvey replaced this idea with circulation.
126702.m: Galen believed the liver was the source of the blood.

126703.q: Which structures in the veins helped Harvey show that the blood there flows towards the heart?
126703.e: Valves in the veins only let blood through towards the heart. Harvey showed this with experiments in which he blocked the blood flow in the arm.
126703.m: Valves in the veins make sure the blood in the veins flows towards the heart.

126704.q: Which connecting link in the circulation was Harvey himself not yet able to prove?
126704.e: Harvey had to assume that blood passed from the arteries into the veins by an invisible route. The tiny hair-like vessels only became visible with the microscope.
126704.m: The capillaries connect arteries and veins, but they were still invisible to Harvey.

126705.q: Which Italian researcher closed the gap in Harvey's circulation in 1661 with observations under the microscope?
126705.e: The Italian Malpighi observed in a frog's lung how arteries and veins are connected to each other.
126705.m: Malpighi confirmed Harvey's circulation with the microscope.

126706.q: Whose personal physician was William Harvey?
126706.e: Harvey was personal physician to James I and then to Charles I of England.
126706.m: Harvey worked as personal physician at the English royal court.

126707.q: Which skin incision for thyroid operations is named after Theodor Kocher?
a: The transverse collar incision on the neck
The vertical incision on the breastbone
The curved incision under the chin
126707.e: Kocher opened the neck with a curved transverse incision in a skin fold above the breastbone. The scar is then hardly noticeable later.
126707.m: The Kocher collar incision leaves an inconspicuous scar on the neck.

126708.q: In which city was Theodor Kocher professor of surgery for decades?
126708.e: From 1872 Kocher ran the surgical clinic at the Inselspital in Bern. He stayed in Bern despite offers from abroad.
126708.m: Theodor Kocher worked at the Inselspital in Bern.

126709.q: Which thyroid condition did Kocher operate on particularly often?
126709.e: A goitre is an enlargement of the thyroid gland. Kocher carried out thousands of goitre operations.
126709.m: Kocher was a master of the goitre operation.

126710.q: Why was goitre widespread in Switzerland in Kocher's time?
a: Because of a lack of iodine in the soil and food
Because of too much table salt
126710.e: In Alpine regions, the soil and water contain little iodine. Without iodine, the thyroid gland gets bigger.
126710.m: A lack of iodine makes the thyroid grow into a goitre.

126711.q: What did Kocher observe in patients whose thyroid gland had been completely removed?
a: Severe signs of an underactive thyroid
126711.e: The patients became sluggish, slow-moving and mentally slowed down. Kocher concluded that the thyroid is vital and from then on always left part of it in place.
126711.m: Kocher recognised that the body needs the thyroid to live.

126712.q: How did Kocher change the death rate in goitre operations?
a: It fell to below one per cent
126712.e: Thanks to precise technique, careful control of bleeding and asepsis, Kocher lowered the death rate from very high levels to less than one per cent.
126712.m: Through careful technique, Kocher made the goitre operation safe.

126713.q: Which surgical instrument bears Theodor Kocher's name?
126713.e: The Kocher clamp is a clamp with toothed tips used to grip tissue and blood vessels. It is still used today.
126713.m: The Kocher clamp is still part of the surgical kit today.

126714.q: What is the so-called Kocher manoeuvre used for?
a: Putting a dislocated shoulder back in place
126714.e: In the Kocher manoeuvre, the arm is rotated and guided in a set sequence until the head of the upper arm bone slides back into the joint socket.
126714.m: The Kocher manoeuvre puts a shoulder back in place.

126715.q: What was Salvarsan, developed by Paul Ehrlich?
126715.e: Salvarsan was an arsenic compound that specifically killed a bacterial pathogen. It came onto the market in 1910.
126715.m: Salvarsan was one of the first artificially produced remedies against pathogens.

126716.q: Which image did Ehrlich use to describe a medicine that only hits the pathogen?
126716.e: Ehrlich looked for substances that, like a “magic bullet”, only hit the pathogen and spare the body. This idea still shapes drug research today.
126716.m: Ehrlich's magic bullet stands for a medicine that specifically hits only the pathogen.

126717.q: For which field of research did Paul Ehrlich receive the Nobel Prize in Medicine in 1908?
126717.e: Ehrlich was honoured together with Élie Metchnikoff for work on immunity. Metchnikoff had described the phagocytes.
126717.m: Ehrlich received the Nobel Prize for research on immunity.

126718.q: Which medical term did Paul Ehrlich coin?
126718.e: Ehrlich called the treatment of diseases with specifically acting chemical substances “chemotherapy”.
126718.m: The word chemotherapy goes back to Paul Ehrlich.

126719.q: Which defence substances of the immune system did Paul Ehrlich try to explain with his side-chain theory?
126719.e: According to Ehrlich, cells carry “side chains” to which toxins bind. If these are made in excess and released, they act as antibodies.
126719.m: Ehrlich's side-chain theory was an early model of how antibodies are formed.

126720.q: What did Paul Ehrlich use to make different cells distinguishable under the microscope?
126720.e: Ehrlich stained blood and tissue with aniline dyes. This let him tell different white blood cells apart, and he discovered mast cells.
126720.m: Ehrlich made cells visible with dyes.

126721.q: For which therapeutic serum did Ehrlich develop a method to determine its exact strength?
126721.e: Ehrlich created methods for measuring and comparing the strength of the diphtheria antitoxin. Only then could the serum be dosed reliably.
126721.m: Ehrlich made diphtheria serum measurable and so safe to dose.

126722.q: Which of Ehrlich's observations is seen as an early clue to the blood-brain barrier?
a: Dyes in the blood did not stain the brain
126722.e: Ehrlich injected dyes into the blood of laboratory animals. Almost all organs were stained, but not the brain.
126722.m: The brain is shielded from the blood by a barrier.

126723.q: What is the name of Haller's famous poem from 1729?
126723.e: In “Die Alpen”, Haller contrasted the simple life of mountain people with the luxury of the cities. The poem shaped the image of the Swiss Alps in Europe.
126723.m: Haller's poem “Die Alpen” made the Swiss mountains famous.

126724.q: At which newly founded university of the time did Haller teach for many years?
126724.e: In 1736 Haller was appointed to the young University of Göttingen. There he taught anatomy, botany and surgery.
126724.m: Haller made the University of Göttingen a centre of medicine.

126725.q: Which property did Haller attribute to muscle fibres?
126725.e: Haller showed in experiments that muscles contract in response to a stimulus. He called this responsiveness irritability.
126725.m: According to Haller, muscles respond to stimuli: they have irritability.

126726.q: What did Haller mean by the “sensibility” of a tissue?
a: The ability to feel stimuli through nerves
126726.e: Haller distinguished sensitive tissues, which contain nerves, from irritable muscles. In doing so he was the first to clearly separate nerve and muscle function.
126726.m: For Haller, sensibility means feeling through nerves.

126727.q: Albrecht von Haller is often regarded as the founder of which field?
126727.e: In his great work “Elementa physiologiae corporis humani”, Haller summarised what was known about the body's functions and based it on experiments.
126727.m: Haller turned physiology into an experimental science.

126728.q: Which Swiss living things did Haller deal with in a large collected work?
126728.e: Haller was also an important botanist. He described the flora of Switzerland in an extensive work.
126728.m: Haller was not only a doctor but also a great expert on Swiss plants.

126729.q: On which Swiss banknote of the sixth series was Albrecht von Haller shown?
126729.e: The sixth banknote series of the National Bank honoured scientists and artists. Haller appeared on the 500-franc note.
126729.m: Albrecht von Haller once appeared on the 500-franc note.

126730.q: Which hormone did Frederick Banting and his team discover in 1921?
126730.e: In 1921 the team obtained a substance from animal organs that lowers blood sugar.
126730.m: Banting discovered insulin together with his team.

126731.q: Which young student did Banting work with on the discovery of insulin?
126731.e: Charles Best was a medical student and helped Banting with the experiments on dogs in the summer of 1921.
126731.m: Charles Best was Banting's most important helper in the insulin experiments.

126732.q: Who did Banting share the Nobel Prize in Medicine with in 1923?
126732.e: The prize went to Banting and the head of the institute, John Macleod. In protest, Banting shared his prize money with Best.
126732.m: Banting and Macleod received the Nobel Prize for insulin.

126733.q: What is still special today about Banting's 1923 Nobel Prize?
a: He is the youngest winner of the prize for medicine
He received it after his death
126733.e: Banting was only 32 years old when it was awarded. No other Nobel laureate in Physiology or Medicine has been younger.
126733.m: Banting is the youngest Nobel laureate in medicine.

126734.q: Which disease became treatable thanks to the discovery of insulin?
126734.e: In type 1 diabetes, the body no longer produces insulin. Before 1922, the disease almost always led to death.
126734.m: Insulin saves the lives of people with type 1 diabetes.

126735.q: From which organ did Banting and Best obtain their insulin?
126735.e: Insulin is made in the islets of Langerhans in the pancreas. The researchers obtained extracts from the pancreases of animals.

126736.q: After 1922, how did people with type 1 diabetes have to receive their insulin?
a: As an injection under the skin
As an ointment on the skin
126736.e: Insulin is a protein and would be digested in the stomach. That is why it has to be injected, today often with pens or pumps.
126736.m: Insulin is injected because it would be digested in the stomach.

126737.q: What did the discoverers of insulin do with their patent?
a: They sold it for a symbolic sum
They sold it to a company for a lot of money
126737.e: The inventors handed over the rights to the University of Toronto for a symbolic sum. Insulin was to be available to all patients.
126737.m: The insulin patent was practically given away so that everyone could benefit.

126738.q: Why did the first insulin extracts cause problems for patients in 1922?
a: They had been stored too cold
126738.e: The first extracts from pancreases still contained many foreign substances and triggered defensive reactions. Only a better purification process made the treatment safe.
126738.m: Insulin first had to be purified before it worked safely.

126739.q: Which substance did Joseph Lister use to fight wound infections?
126739.e: Lister treated wounds, dressings and instruments with carbolic acid, also called phenol. This killed germs.
126739.m: Lister fought germs in wounds with carbolic acid.

126740.q: Whose research gave Lister the idea of killing germs in wounds?
126740.e: Pasteur had shown that microorganisms cause fermentation and rotting. Lister applied this finding to festering wounds.
126740.m: Pasteur's germ theory was the basis for Lister's antiseptic method.

126741.q: In which city did Lister begin his antiseptic method in the 1860s?
126741.e: Lister was a surgeon at the Royal Infirmary in Glasgow. From 1865 he treated wounds there with carbolic acid.

126742.q: On which type of injury did Lister first try out his method?
126742.e: At that time, open fractures often became so inflamed that the limb had to be amputated. With carbolic acid, a boy's wound healed without pus forming.
126742.m: Lister's first success was an open fracture that healed without infection.

126743.q: Which device did Lister use in the operating theatre to kill germs in the air?
126743.e: Lister had carbolic acid sprayed into the air during operations. Later it was recognised that germs are mainly spread by hands and instruments.
126743.m: Lister even tried to spray the air in the operating theatre free of germs.

126744.q: Which problem after operations was Lister able to greatly reduce with his method?
126744.e: Before Lister, many patients died after operations from festering wounds and blood poisoning. His antiseptic method lowered this death rate considerably.
126744.m: Lister's antiseptic method made operations far less dangerous.

126745.q: How does Lister's antisepsis differ from later asepsis?
a: Antisepsis kills germs, asepsis keeps them away
126745.e: Lister killed germs in the wound with chemicals. In asepsis, sterile instruments and clothing prevent germs from getting in at all.
126745.m: Antisepsis fights germs that are present, asepsis stops them getting in.

126746.q: Which genus of bacteria was named in honour of Joseph Lister?
126746.e: The genus Listeria bears Lister's name. These bacteria can cause the disease listeriosis through food.
126746.m: The bacteria of the genus Listeria are named after Joseph Lister.

126747.q: In which city did the first public operation under ether anaesthesia take place in 1846?
126747.e: On 16 October 1846, a tumour on the neck was removed painlessly at Massachusetts General Hospital in Boston. The day is regarded as the birth of modern anaesthesia.
126747.m: Modern anaesthesia began in Boston in 1846.

126748.q: Who gave the ether during the famous demonstration in Boston in 1846?
126748.e: The dentist William Morton had the patient breathe in ether vapour. The surgeon operated without the patient showing any pain.
126748.m: William Morton demonstrated ether anaesthesia in public.

126749.q: What great advance did ether anaesthesia bring for surgery?
a: Operations without pain for the patients
Operations without the risk of infection
126749.e: Before, operations had to be done with the patient fully conscious and as quickly as possible. With anaesthesia, surgeons could operate more carefully and for longer. Only antisepsis helped against infections.

126750.q: Which chemical compound is the classic anaesthetic ether?
126750.e: Anaesthetic ether is diethyl ether, a highly volatile liquid. Breathing in its vapour causes unconsciousness.
126750.m: The chemical name of anaesthetic ether is diethyl ether.

126751.q: Which drawback made ether dangerous in the operating theatre?
126751.e: Ether vapour forms explosive mixtures with air. Naked flames and sparks were therefore dangerous in the operating theatre.
126751.m: Ether vapour can easily catch fire.

126752.q: Which anaesthetic did James Young Simpson introduce in Edinburgh in 1847?
126752.e: Simpson was looking for an alternative to ether and found chloroform. It worked quickly but was more dangerous for the heart and liver.
126752.m: Shortly after ether, chloroform came into use as an anaesthetic.

126753.q: Which gas was already used to relieve pain in the 19th century and is still used today?
126753.e: Laughing gas (nitrous oxide) was tried out by dentists in the 1840s. Today it is used against pain during childbirth, at the dentist's or by the ambulance service, for example.
126753.m: Laughing gas has relieved pain since the 19th century.

126754.q: What does the Greek word “anaesthesia” mean?
126754.e: “An” means “not” and “aisthesis” means “sensation”. The term came into use in 1846, shortly after the first ether anaesthesia.

126755.q: At which Basel company was ciclosporin discovered and developed?
126755.e: Researchers at Sandoz in Basel discovered the effect of the substance in the early 1970s. Sandoz later became part of Novartis.
126755.m: Ciclosporin is a discovery of Basel pharmaceutical research.

126756.q: What kind of living thing does ciclosporin originally come from?
126756.e: Ciclosporin is produced by the sac fungus Tolypocladium inflatum. It was found in a soil sample.
126756.m: Ciclosporin is a natural substance from a soil fungus.

126757.q: Where did pharmaceutical researchers look for new active substances in the 1970s and so find the ciclosporin fungus?
