127935.q: Lea is moving to a different municipality. Where does she deregister?
a: With the federal government in Bern
127935.e: Anyone moving away deregisters with the residents' registration office of the old municipality. In the new municipality you register within the deadline.
127935.m: Deregister in the old municipality, register in the new one.

127936.q: How long is the probation period after passing the driving test in Switzerland?
127936.e: After passing the test you receive a probationary driving licence for 3 years. For serious offences it can be extended or cancelled.

127937.q: What alcohol limit applies to new drivers with a probationary licence?
127937.e: For new drivers and learners there is practically a ban on alcohol, with a limit of 0.1 per mille. For other drivers the limit is 0.5 per mille.

127938.q: What do you need before you can apply for a learner's permit for a car?
127938.e: The first aid course is a requirement for applying for the learner's permit. There you learn first aid on the road.
127938.m: First aid first, then the learner's permit.

127939.q: From what age can you ride a moped with category M?
127939.e: At 14 you can get a category M licence after a theory test. Wearing a helmet is compulsory on a moped.

127940.q: What is the maximum speed a moped is built to reach?
127940.e: A moped is built so that it reaches at most 30 km/h. Faster vehicles need a different licence category.

127941.q: Under the Data Protection Act, what can you ask a company for?
a: Information about what data it holds about you
127941.e: Everyone has a right to information about their own personal data. The information is usually free of charge.
127941.m: I have the right to know what is stored about me.

127942.q: Who supervises data protection at federal level in Switzerland?
a: The Federal Data Protection and Information Commissioner
127942.e: The FDPIC supervises federal offices and private companies in matters of data protection. It can open investigations and advises the public.
127942.m: The FDPIC keeps watch over data.

127943.q: What should you do with out-of-date medicines?
a: Take them back to the chemist
127943.e: Medicines must not go into the waste water or on the compost. Chemists and pharmacies take them back and dispose of them properly.
127943.m: Old medicines go back to the chemist.

127944.q: Where is the best place to keep the medicine cabinet?
a: Dry, cool and out of children's reach
On the floor of the damp bathroom
127944.e: Damp and heat can spoil medicines. Small children must not be able to get at medicines.

127945.q: A household has neither a television nor a radio. Does it have to pay the media licence fee?
a: Yes, it basically applies to every household
127945.e: Since 2019 the fee has been linked to the household, not to devices. People receiving supplementary benefits, for example, can be exempted.

127946.q: How long can you collect a registered letter after receiving a collection notice?
127946.e: Swiss Post keeps registered items for 7 days. For letters from authorities, a letter often counts as delivered on the last day of this period.
127946.m: Registered post: seven days to collect.

127947.q: What is the difference between A Post and B Post?
a: A Post arrives faster and costs more
B Post is only for parcels
You have to collect B Post yourself
127947.e: A Post letters usually arrive the next working day. B Post is cheaper but takes a few working days longer.
127947.m: A is fast, B is cheap.

127948.q: You have lost your identity card. What must you do?
a: Report the loss to the police
Nothing, it will soon be invalid
127948.e: A lost identity document must be reported to the police. It is then blocked in the search system so that nobody can misuse it.
127948.m: ID gone? Go to the police.

127949.q: What does a bank mainly do?
a: It looks after money and lends money
127949.e: A bank looks after the money of lots of people. It also lends money, for example for a house.

127950.q: Who helps you at the counter in the bank?
a: A police officer with a dog
127950.e: Bank clerks work at the counter. They answer questions and help you pay in or withdraw money.
127950.m: At the bank counter, experts help you.

127951.q: What do you call a person who keeps their money at a bank?
127951.e: Anyone who has an account at a bank is a customer there.
127951.m: If you have an account, you are a customer of the bank.

127952.q: The Meier family wants to buy a house but does not have enough money. What can the bank do?
127952.e: Banks lend money. Later you must pay it back, and usually a bit more than you received.
127952.m: Borrowed money has to be paid back.

127953.q: What is the thick, strong cupboard in the bank for money and valuables called?
127953.e: A safe has thick steel walls and a strong lock. Valuable things are well protected inside.
127953.m: Valuables are safe in the safe.

127954.q: Where does the bank get the money it lends?
a: From the people who put money in their accounts
The Federal Council gives it to them
127954.e: Lots of people put money in their accounts. The bank can lend some of it to others. You still get your money back when you need it.
127954.m: The bank works with savers' money.

a: A place at the bank where your money is recorded
127955.e: In an account, the bank writes down how much money belongs to you. The money is not kept in its own box with your name on.
127955.m: Your account shows how much money belongs to you.

127956.q: Who can open an account for a child up to the age of 9?
a: The parents together with the child
127956.e: Young children need their parents or other guardians to open an account. The parents help and keep an eye on it.
127956.m: For young children, the parents open the account.

127957.q: What does the account balance show?
a: How much money is in the account right now
127957.e: The account balance tells you how much money you have in your account at the moment.
127957.m: The balance shows your money in the account.

127958.q: Mia has 20 francs in her account. She pays in 10 francs. How much does she have now?
127958.e: 20 francs and 10 francs make 30 francs together. Paying in makes the balance bigger.

127959.q: Tim has 50 francs in his account. He withdraws 20 francs. How much is left?
127959.e: 50 francs minus 20 francs is 30 francs. Withdrawing makes the balance smaller.

127960.q: Why does every account have its own number?
a: So the money arrives in the right account
So it can be drawn in the lottery
127960.e: Every account has its own number, the IBAN. That way the bank knows exactly where the money belongs.
127960.m: Every account has its own number.

127961.q: Does the money in your account belong to the bank?
a: Yes, it belongs to the bank
127961.e: The bank only looks after your money. It stays your money and you can take it out again.
127961.m: Your money in the account stays your money.

127962.q: What is a children's or youth account?
a: An account made especially for young people
An account that only works on Sundays
127962.e: Many banks have accounts for children and young people. They help you learn how to handle money.
127962.m: Children can have their own account too.

127963.q: Granny gives Lea 100 francs for her birthday. Lea wants to buy a bike later. Where should the money go?
a: Spend it on sweets straight away
Leave it lying around in her bedroom
Put it in her school desk
127963.e: In the savings account the money is kept safe. When Lea has saved enough, she can buy the bike.
127963.m: For a big goal, use your savings account.

a: A small tin or figure for collecting money
127964.e: In a money box you collect coins and notes at home. That way you can see your savings grow.
127964.m: You collect your money in a money box.

127965.q: Which animal is often the shape of a money box?
127965.e: The piggy bank is very well known. It has a slot on top for the coins.
127965.m: The piggy bank loves eating coins.

127966.q: Why does a money box have a slot on top?
a: So you can put coins and notes in
So you can hang it up
127966.e: You put the money in through the slot. Getting it out is not so easy, which helps you save.
127966.m: Easy to put in, hard to take out.

127967.q: Your money box is full. Where can you take the money so it is kept safe?
a: To the bank, into your savings account
127967.e: When the money box is full, you can take the money to the bank with your parents. There it goes into your account.
127967.m: Full money box? Off to the bank.

127968.q: Noah wants a game that costs 30 francs. He saves 5 francs every week. How many weeks does he need?
127968.e: 5 francs times 6 weeks is 30 francs. With patience, Noah reaches his goal.
127968.m: Small amounts grow big over time.

127969.q: What is the money called that children get regularly from their parents?
127969.e: Many children get pocket money every week or every month. With it they learn to handle money themselves.
127969.m: With pocket money you learn to count and save.

127970.q: Sara gets 4 francs pocket money. She spends 1 franc and saves the rest. How much does she save?
127970.e: 4 francs minus 1 franc is 3 francs. Sara can put them in her money box.
127970.m: What you don't spend, you can save.

a: First think about whether you really need something
Buy everything you see straight away
Empty the money box every day
Always carry money in your pocket
127971.e: Before you buy something, ask yourself: do I really need this? That way more money is left over.

127972.q: What do you really need to live?
127972.e: Every person needs food and drink. Toys are nice, but you can live without them.
127972.m: First what you need, then what is nice.

127973.q: What can you do at a cash machine?
127973.e: At the cash machine you put in your bank card and type your PIN. Then it gives out money from your account.
127973.m: At the cash machine you get cash.

127974.q: What do you need to get money from a cash machine?
a: Your bank card and your PIN
127974.e: The cash machine recognises you by your card. With your secret PIN you show that the card belongs to you.

127975.q: Where does the money from the cash machine come from?
a: It is a present from the bank
127975.e: The money is taken from your account. If there is nothing in the account, there is no money either.
127975.m: The cash machine only gives what is in your account.

127976.q: Someone is standing very close behind you at the cash machine. What do you do?
a: Cover the PIN with your hand or wait
Write the PIN on the screen
127976.e: Nobody should see which numbers you type. Cover the keys with your hand or ask them to step back.
127976.m: Cover the keys while you type.

127977.q: What should you not forget after withdrawing money?
a: To take your card and the money
To say the PIN out loud
To write the PIN on a note
To put the receipt into the machine
127977.e: Always take the card first and then the money. Only then do you walk away.
127977.m: Always take your card and money.

127978.q: Where do you often find a cash machine in Switzerland?
a: At a bank or at the railway station
127978.e: Cash machines are in lots of places: at banks, at railway stations or in shopping centres.
127978.m: Cash machines are where lots of people are.

127979.q: The cash machine keeps your card. What do you do?
a: Just go home and say nothing
127979.e: If the card stays in the machine, your parents or the bank must be told quickly. They know what to do.
127979.m: Problem with your card? Tell someone straight away.

a: A secret number for your card
127980.e: The PIN is a secret number. Only you know it, so nobody else can use your card.

127981.q: Your best friend asks for your PIN. What do you say?
a: I'll write it down for you
I'll tell everyone in the class
127981.e: You never give away your PIN, not even to good friends. That way your money stays protected.
127981.m: Only one person knows the PIN: you.

127982.q: Where is the best place to keep your PIN?
a: On a note in your purse
On a sticker on your phone
127982.e: Otherwise anyone who finds the card and the note could take money. It is best to learn your PIN by heart.
127982.m: Never write your PIN on the card.

127983.q: You have lost your bank card. What do you do first?
a: Tell your parents straight away so the card can be blocked
127983.e: A lost card must be blocked quickly. Then nobody else can pay with it.
127983.m: Card gone? Have it blocked at once.

127984.q: May a stranger borrow your bank card?
a: No, the card belongs only to you
Yes, if he brings it back
127984.e: Your card is only for you. Never give it to a stranger.

127985.q: Which PIN is the worst, because it is easy to guess?
127985.e: Thieves try numbers like 1234 or 0000 first. A good PIN has no simple pattern.
127985.m: A good PIN is not a simple pattern.

127986.q: What is a bank card usually made of?
127986.e: Bank cards are made of strong plastic. They have a small chip that stores important data.
127986.m: A bank card is made of plastic with a chip.

127987.q: What is the small gold or silver part on a bank card?
a: A chip with the card's data
127987.e: The chip stores the card's data. Card readers in shops or at cash machines can read it.
127987.m: The chip is the card's brain.

127988.q: What is the best way to treat your bank card?
a: Keep it in your purse and don't bend it
Carry it loose in your school bag
Give it to your friends to play with
127988.e: A bent or broken card might not work any more. Keep it in your purse or wallet.
127988.m: Take good care of your card.

127989.q: How many digits does a bank card PIN often have?
127989.e: A PIN usually has 4 or 6 digits. That makes it easy to remember.
127989.m: A PIN is short but secret.

a: Taking money out of your account
127990.e: When you pay in, money goes into your account. Your balance gets bigger.
127990.m: Paying in: money goes into the account.

a: Taking money out of your account
127991.e: When you withdraw, you take money out of your account, for example at a cash machine. Your balance gets smaller.
127991.m: Withdrawing: money comes out of the account.

127992.q: Where can you pay cash into an account?
a: At the bank counter or a deposit machine
127992.e: You can hand in cash at the counter or pay it in at special machines. Then it goes into your account.
127992.m: You pay in cash at the bank.

127993.q: Ben has 10 francs in his account and wants to withdraw 50 francs. What happens?
a: It doesn't work, because there is not enough money
127993.e: You can only withdraw what is in the account. The account cannot give out more than it holds.
127993.m: You can only take out what is there.

127994.q: Lars pays in 5 francs, then another 5 francs. Before that, the account was empty. How much is in it?
127994.e: 5 and 5 make 10. Every payment in makes the balance bigger.
127994.m: Lots of small payments add up to a lot.

a: A slip of paper showing what was paid
127995.e: A receipt shows how much money was paid or paid in. It is proof.

127996.q: What is the small amount of money the bank sometimes gives you when your money stays in a savings account for a long time?
127996.e: The bank sometimes pays you a small amount for keeping your money there. This is called interest.
127996.m: Interest is a small thank you for saving.

127997.q: Your parents borrow money from the bank. Who has to pay interest?
127997.e: Whoever borrows money from the bank later pays back more than they received. The extra is the interest.

127998.q: Leonie has saved 100 francs. At the end of the year there are 101 francs in her account. Where does the extra franc come from?
a: It is interest from the bank
127998.e: The bank has paid Leonie interest. That is a small amount for the money she saved.
127998.m: Saved money can grow a little.

127999.q: Which statement about interest on a savings account is true?
a: It is often only a small amount
It makes you rich straight away
127999.e: Interest on a savings account is usually small. But over many years it can add up.
127999.m: Interest is small, but over time it counts.

128000.q: What happens with interest if you keep your money in a money box at home?
128000.e: Only the bank can pay interest. In the money box, the money stays exactly the same.
128000.m: Money does not grow in a money box.

a: Coins and notes you can touch
128001.e: Cash means coins and banknotes. You can hold them in your hand and count them.

128002.q: What can you pay with in a shop?
128002.e: In a shop you pay with coins and notes or with a card. Sometimes you can use your phone too.

128003.q: What is one advantage of cash?
a: You can see exactly how much money you have left
You can pay with it in any country
128003.e: With cash in your purse you can see at once how much is left. That helps you not to spend too much.
128003.m: Cash shows you clearly what you have.

128004.q: What happens when you pay with your bank card in a shop?
a: The money is taken from your account
You get the things for free
The card goes empty and breaks
128004.e: When you pay by card, the bank takes the money from your account and gives it to the shop.
128004.m: Card money is real money too.

128005.q: What is a disadvantage of only paying by card?
a: You notice less how much you are spending
You can only buy small things
You have to count the coins yourself
128005.e: With a card the money flows away invisibly. That is why it is easier to lose track.

128006.q: What do you keep coins, notes and cards in when you are out?
a: In a PE bag with no zip
128006.e: A purse or wallet keeps your money and your card together. That way nothing gets lost.
128006.m: Money belongs in a purse or wallet.

128007.q: You pay for an ice cream costing 3 francs with a 5-franc coin. How much change do you get?
128007.e: 5 francs minus 3 francs is 2 francs. That is your change.

128008.q: What does contactless payment by card mean?
a: Just holding the card briefly to the reader
Putting the card into the reader
Giving the card to the shop assistant
128008.e: For small amounts you hold the card briefly against the card reader. For larger amounts you usually have to enter your PIN.

128009.q: Which coin has the highest value in Switzerland?
128009.e: The five-franc coin, or Fünfliber, has the highest value. It is also the biggest and heaviest Swiss coin.
128009.m: The five-franc coin is the biggest coin.

128011.q: Which Swiss coin is golden yellow?
128011.e: The 5-centime coin shines golden yellow. The other coins are silvery.

128012.q: What is the 5-franc coin often called in Switzerland?
128012.e: Fünfliber is an old, popular name for the 5-franc coin.

128013.q: Which Swiss banknote has the lowest value?
128013.e: The smallest banknote is the 10-franc note. For 5 francs there is a coin.
128013.m: The smallest note is the 10-franc note.

128014.q: Which Swiss banknote has the highest value?
128014.e: The biggest note is the 1000-franc note. It is purple. There is no 500-franc note in Switzerland.

128015.e: There are notes of 10, 20, 50, 100, 200 and 1000 francs. The 200-franc note is brown.

128016.q: How many different banknotes are there in Switzerland?

128017.e: 50 centimes and 50 centimes make 100 centimes, which is 1 franc.

128018.e: 5 times 20 centimes is 100 centimes, which is 1 franc.

128019.e: 10 times 10 centimes is 100 centimes, which is 1 franc.

128020.q: How many 10-franc notes are worth the same as a 100-franc note?

128021.q: How many 20-franc notes are worth the same as a 100-franc note?

128022.q: Which is worth more: a 2-franc coin or four 50-centime coins?
128022.e: Four times 50 centimes is 200 centimes, which is 2 francs. Both are the same.
128022.m: Same amount of money, different coins.

128023.q: You have a 1-franc coin and a 50-centime coin. How much money is that?
128023.e: 1 franc and 50 centimes together make 1 franc 50 centimes.
128023.m: Add up the francs and the centimes.

128024.q: Which woman can you see on the 1-franc coin?
128024.e: The standing woman on the coin is Helvetia. She is a symbol of Switzerland.

a: Copied money that is not real
128025.e: Counterfeit money is copied and illegal. Real notes have special security features.
128025.m: Counterfeit money is not real money.

128026.q: Why do banknotes glitter and shimmer in some places?
a: To make them hard to copy
To make them glow in the dark
So you can find them faster in your purse
128026.e: Glittering parts and special pictures are security features. They make it hard to forge notes.

128027.q: What do you pay with when you use TWINT?
128027.e: TWINT is an app on your phone. You can use it to pay in shops or send money to other people.

128028.q: Where does the money come from when you pay with TWINT?
128028.e: TWINT is linked to a bank account. The money is taken from there.
128028.m: TWINT money is real money too.

128029.q: What can you do with TWINT?
128029.e: With TWINT you can send money to another person who has TWINT, for example for a shared present.
128029.m: With TWINT you can pass money on quickly.

128030.q: How do you often pay with TWINT in a shop?
a: You scan a code with your phone
128030.e: In shops the till often shows a QR code. You scan it with the TWINT app and confirm the amount.

128031.q: Who should be there when a child uses TWINT for the first time?
128031.e: The parents help set it up and explain how to pay safely.
128031.m: Try out new money apps with your parents.

128032.q: Someone you don't know sends you a TWINT request for money. What do you do?
a: Decline it and show your parents
128032.e: You only pay people you know, and when you know what for. With strangers, always ask your parents.
128032.m: Unknown request? Don't pay, ask your parents.

128033.q: Why does the TWINT app have a code or fingerprint to unlock it?
a: So that only you can pay with it
To make the phone look nicer
128033.e: The code protects your money. If someone takes your phone, they cannot pay without the code.
128033.m: The app code protects your money.

128034.q: Your purse has gone. What is a good thing to do?
128034.e: If there was a card in the purse, it must be blocked quickly. Your parents will help you.

128035.q: On the phone, someone says they are from the bank and asks for your PIN. What do you do?
a: Give nothing away and hang up
128035.e: A real bank never asks for your PIN. Hang up and tell your parents.
128035.m: The bank never asks for your PIN.

128036.q: You find a purse in the street. What do you do?
a: Hand it in, for example at the lost property office or the police
128036.e: Things you find belong to someone else. Hand it in with a grown-up at the lost property office or the police.
128036.m: You hand in things you find.

128037.q: Where is your purse safest on the bus?
a: In a closed bag close to your body
Open on the seat next to you
Hanging on the outside of your rucksack
In your hand, high in the air
128037.e: In a closed bag close to you, nobody can simply take it.
128037.m: Carry money close to your body.

128039.q: Something strange is stuck onto the cash machine. What do you do?
a: Not put your card in and tell a grown-up
Pull the thing off and take it
128039.e: Sometimes fraudsters stick devices onto cash machines. If something looks strange, don't use the machine.

128040.q: Lena is 12 and would like her own account. What is usually best for her?
a: A youth account with low or no fees
A mortgage with a fixed rate
An account with a high credit limit
128040.e: Banks offer special accounts for children and young people. They are often free of fees and cannot go overdrawn.

128041.q: What usually happens if you try to spend more than is in a youth account?
a: The bank gives you the missing amount
128041.e: Youth accounts usually cannot be overdrawn. That way young people cannot get into debt on their account.
128041.m: No money in it, no payment.

128042.q: What often happens to a youth account when you get older and reach the age limit?
a: It is turned into a normal personal account
It is closed and the money is lost
It goes to the National Bank
It turns into a piggy bank
128042.e: Youth accounts only apply up to a certain age. After that the account is usually turned into a personal account with different conditions.
128042.m: The account grows up with you.

128043.q: What is a personal current account mainly for?
128043.e: For example, your wages go into your current account, and you pay bills and shopping from it. A savings account is better for saving.
128043.m: Current account for paying, savings account for saving.

128044.q: Which statement about a savings account is usually true?
a: You cannot withdraw as much as you like at once
You get a free credit card with it
You pay all your bills from it
128044.e: Many savings accounts have limits on how much you can withdraw per month without giving notice. In return, the interest is often a bit higher than on a current account.
128044.m: Savings account: let the money rest.

128045.q: Nico puts 20 francs into his savings account every month. How much has he saved after one year, without interest?
128045.e: A year has 12 months. 12 times 20 francs makes 240 francs.
128045.m: Small amounts add up to big ones.

128046.q: Why is it worth putting money into a savings account rather than a piggy bank?
a: It is safer and can earn interest
The bank adds 100 francs every year
You can withdraw unlimited amounts at any time
You never have to think about the money again
128046.e: In a savings account the money is protected against theft and loss. The bank also pays interest, depending on interest rates.
128046.m: Money in the bank does a little work too.

128047.q: Mia pays in a shop with her debit card. When is the money taken from her account?
a: Straight away or within a few days
128047.e: With a debit card the amount is taken directly from your own account. So you can only spend what is there.
128047.m: Debit: the money goes straight away.

128048.q: How do you normally pay for shopping done with a credit card?
a: Not at all, the bank covers it
Each purchase separately at the counter
128048.e: With a credit card, the company collects all your purchases and sends a bill once a month. You must pay it on time.
128048.m: Credit means: buy first, pay later.

128049.q: What happens if you only pay part of your credit card bill?
a: High interest is charged on the rest
The rest is automatically let off
The card becomes twice as big
128049.e: If you only pay part, the rest counts as a loan. Credit card companies charge high interest on it.
128049.m: Always pay off your credit card in full.

a: A card you first have to top up with money
A card you can pay with without limit
A card only for cash machines abroad
A card that never has a PIN
128050.e: Prepaid means “paid in advance”. You can only spend as much as you have loaded onto it.

128051.q: From what age do people in Switzerland usually get a real credit card?
a: From the first day of school
128051.e: For a credit card you must be an adult, and the bank checks your income. Younger people get at most a prepaid or debit card.

128052.q: What does the wave symbol on a bank card mean?
a: The card only works at the seaside
128052.e: With the wave symbol you just hold the card briefly against the payment terminal. For small amounts you often don't need a PIN.

128053.q: Why do you still have to enter your PIN now and then when paying contactless?
a: For protection in case the card has been stolen
So the card is topped up again
So the shop pays lower fees
128053.e: Above a certain amount or after several payments, the terminal asks for the PIN. That way a thief cannot spend as much as they like.
128053.m: The PIN is the card's lock.

128054.q: Leon has lost his bank card. What should he do straight away?
a: Have the card blocked by the bank
Wait a week to see if it turns up
Post the PIN on social media
Open a new account at another bank
128054.e: You should have a lost card blocked at once, by phone or in the app. Then nobody can pay with it any more.
128054.m: Card gone? Block it at once!

128055.q: What is the three-digit number on the back of many cards?
a: A security code for internet payments
The number of purchases per day
128055.e: The security code, often called CVV, is needed when buying online. Only enter it in secure shops and never give it to strangers on the phone.
128055.m: The back of the card stays secret.

a: A random number that has nothing to do with you
128056.e: Thieves can easily guess simple sequences and dates of birth. A random PIN is much harder to crack.

128057.q: What usually happens if you enter the wrong PIN three times?
a: The card gives out more money
Nothing, you can keep trying for ever
128057.e: After several wrong attempts, the bank blocks the card. That way a thief cannot simply try out PINs.

128058.q: Why do you cover the keypad with your hand when typing your PIN?
a: So nobody can spy on your PIN
128058.e: Thieves sometimes look over your shoulder or film secretly. With your hand covering the keys, your PIN stays secret.
128058.m: Hand over the keys, PIN stays secret.

128059.q: Is it all right to write your PIN on the card so you don't forget it?
a: No, otherwise a finder can use the card at once
Yes, if the card is new
128059.e: If the PIN is on the card, a thief has everything they need. You then often have to pay for any loss yourself.
128059.m: PIN in your head, not on the card.

128060.e: The PIN is personal. Even the bank never asks for it, neither on the phone nor by email.
128060.m: My PIN belongs only to me.

128061.q: What should you do if a cash machine looks odd, for example with a loose card slot?
a: Not use it and inform the bank
Quickly put your card in anyway
128061.e: Fraudsters sometimes fit devices to cash machines that copy card data. This is called skimming.

128062.q: What is the trick called where fraudsters copy card data at a cash machine?
128062.e: With skimming, a reader is fitted over the card slot, often with a mini camera for the PIN. This is used to make fake cards.

128063.q: Why can withdrawing money from another bank's cash machine cost something?
a: Some banks charge a fee for it
Because the money there is older
Because other machines only give coins
Because you get twice as much there
128063.e: At your own bank, withdrawing is usually free. At other machines or abroad, fees may apply.
128063.m: Using your own bank's machine saves fees.

128064.q: What should you do first after withdrawing money?
a: Put your card and money away at once
Count the money out loud in front of everyone
Leave the card in the machine
Take a photo of the PIN
128064.e: Put your card and cash away safely straight away. Counting for ages attracts thieves.

128065.q: On TWINT, what are you usually found by when someone wants to send you money?
128065.e: On TWINT you can send money to contacts in your phone book. The mobile number is used to identify you.
128065.m: TWINT knows you by your mobile number.

128067.q: Jana paid for everyone's cinema tickets. How can she get the money back from her friends with TWINT?
a: She has to send a bill by post
She has to go to the National Bank
128067.e: In TWINT you can request money from contacts. Your friends just have to confirm the request.

128068.q: A stranger asks you on TWINT to confirm a payment request so that you will “receive money”. What is true?
a: Confirming sends your money away, so decline
It is a safe game rule
You have to give away your PIN for it
128068.e: With a payment request, you pay if you confirm. Fraudsters use this trick on selling platforms.

128069.q: What should the TWINT app be protected with?
a: Nothing at all, for faster paying
Your pet's name on the screen
128069.e: Anyone who finds the phone should not be able to simply send money. That is why the app needs a code or fingerprint.

128070.q: What can you do with online banking, for example?
a: See your balance and pay bills
Take money from other people's accounts
128070.e: With online banking you do your banking on a computer or phone. You can see account activity and make payments.
128070.m: Online banking: the bank in your pocket.

128071.q: What should you always do after using online banking?
a: Write down the password and leave it lying around
128071.e: Logging out ends the session. Otherwise someone else could carry on using it on the same device.

128072.q: What is the safest way to open online banking?
a: Type the address yourself or use the official app
Click a link in an unknown email
Through an advert in a game
Through a link in a text message
128072.e: Links in messages can lead to fake websites. If you type the address yourself, you safely reach the real bank.
128072.m: Type it yourself instead of clicking.

128073.q: Why should you not do online banking on a public computer?
a: Other people's devices can read your data
Because public computers are too slow
Because your account will then be deleted
Because only games run on them
128073.e: Other devices could have malware installed that records passwords. It is better to do your banking on your own device.
128073.m: Do your banking only on your own device.

a: A bill that comes straight into your online banking
A game run by the National Bank
128074.e: With eBill you receive bills digitally in your online banking. You check them and approve payment with one click.

128075.q: What do you need an IBAN for?
a: So that money reaches the right account
To buy chewing gum at the kiosk
As a password for online banking
128075.e: The IBAN is the international account number. Anyone who wants to transfer money to you needs your IBAN.

128076.q: How many characters does a Swiss IBAN have?
128076.e: A Swiss IBAN has 21 characters: CH, two check digits, the bank's number and the account number.

128077.q: Is it all right to give out your IBAN so that you can receive money?
a: Yes, nobody can withdraw money with it
No, otherwise the account is emptied at once
128077.e: With an IBAN people can pay money into an account, but cannot take any out. Your PIN and passwords, on the other hand, stay secret.
128077.m: Share your IBAN, yes; your PIN, never.

128078.q: What comes in a Swiss IBAN after “CH” and the two check digits?
a: A number for the bank, then the account number
128078.e: After the country code and the check digits comes the bank's number. Then comes the actual account number.

128079.q: What are the two check digits in an IBAN for?
a: They help to spot typing mistakes
They show the age of the account
128079.e: If an IBAN is typed wrongly, the check digits no longer match. The online banking then shows an error.

128080.q: Which letters does the IBAN of an account in Liechtenstein start with?
128080.e: Every country has its own code. For Liechtenstein it is LI, for Switzerland CH.

128081.q: What do you need at least to transfer money to someone?
128081.e: For a transfer you give the IBAN, the name and the amount. You never need the other person's passwords or PIN.
128081.m: IBAN, name, amount: off it goes.

128082.q: What is the difference between a deposit and a transfer?
a: A deposit uses cash, a transfer goes from account to account
There is no difference between them
A transfer only works with coins
128082.e: For a deposit you take cash to the bank or post office. A transfer sends money without cash from one account to another.

128083.q: What is a credit to your account?
a: Money going out of the account
128083.e: A credit increases your balance, for example when your wages arrive. The opposite is a debit.

128084.q: Which payment is a standing order best suited to?
128084.e: A standing order regularly pays the same amount to the same person. That suits rent or pocket money well.

128085.q: Where can you pay cash into an account in Switzerland?
a: At the bank counter or a deposit machine
128085.e: You can pay in cash at the counter or at special machines. You can also do it at post office counters.
128085.m: Cash in, at the counter or a machine.

128086.q: Why should you check everything again before confirming a transfer?
a: Getting money back from a wrong transfer is difficult
Because otherwise the bank charges a fine
Because otherwise the transfer is made twice
Because otherwise you get more interest
128086.e: Once the money is in the wrong account, you have to go to a lot of trouble to claim it back. A careful look at the IBAN and amount saves hassle.

128087.q: What is shown in the middle of the QR code on a Swiss QR-bill?
128087.e: The Swiss cross shows that it is a QR code for Swiss bills. That way you recognise it at once.

128088.q: What is a particularly easy way to pay a QR-bill?
a: Scan the QR code with your banking app
Type in all the details by hand
Put the bill into a cash machine
Send the amount in cash in a letter
128088.e: The banking app reads the IBAN, amount and reference from the QR code. You only have to check and confirm.

128089.q: Which details are contained in the QR code of a QR-bill?
a: The IBAN, the recipient and the amount, among others
128089.e: The code contains all the payment details. That way no typing mistakes happen when entering them.
128089.m: The whole payment is in the code.

128090.q: Can you pay a QR-bill without a phone?
a: Yes, for example at the post office counter
No, only with a banking app
No, only with a credit card
128090.e: The payment part of the QR-bill can also be paid at the post office counter or with a payment order.
128090.m: A QR-bill can be paid digitally or at the counter.

128091.q: Since which year has the QR-bill existed in Switzerland?
128091.e: The QR-bill came in in 2020. By autumn 2022 it had completely replaced the old payment slips.
128091.m: In 2020 the QR code came onto bills.

128092.q: Tim has 500 francs in his savings account. The bank pays 1% interest per year. How much interest does he get after one year?
128092.e: 1% of 500 francs is 500 divided by 100, which is 5 francs.

128093.q: Who pays interest when someone takes out a loan from the bank?
128093.e: Whoever borrows money pays the bank interest as the price for the borrowed money. That is how the bank earns money.

128094.q: Why does the bank pay interest on savings?
a: Because it can lend the money on
Because the government pays it back
Because otherwise it may not print banknotes
Because it only stores the money
128094.e: The bank lends part of the savings to others, for example for houses. It receives interest for the lending and passes some of it on.
128094.m: The bank works with your savings.

128095.q: Which statement about interest is true?
a: Loan interest is usually higher than savings interest
Savings interest is always higher than loan interest
128095.e: The bank charges more interest for loans than it pays to savers. The bank lives on the difference.
128095.m: Borrowing costs more than saving earns.

a: An amount the bank charges for running the account
A birthday present from the bank
A fine for saving too much
128096.e: Many banks charge a fee for the account and cards. With youth accounts it is often waived.
128096.m: Running an account can cost something.

128097.q: Why can paying by card abroad cost more?
a: There can be fees for foreign currency
Because the card gets heavier abroad
Because the PIN is longer there
128097.e: If you pay in euros or another currency, the bank converts it. It often charges a fee for this.
128097.m: Foreign currency often means extra costs.

128098.q: Lara wants to compare banks. What does she look at besides interest?
a: The fees for the account and card
The size of the front door
128098.e: Good interest is little use if high fees eat it up. That is why you compare both.
128098.m: Always look at interest and fees together.

128099.q: How can you often recognise a phishing message?
a: It puts you under pressure, for example “Your account will be blocked today!”
It always comes on a Monday
128099.e: Scammers rely on time pressure and fear. Real banks do not threaten by email to block your account at once.
128099.m: Pressure and hurry are warning signs.

128100.e: With smishing, fake text messages arrive, supposedly from the post office or the bank, for example. Never click on links in them.
128100.m: Text message with a link? Careful!

128101.q: A caller says he is from your bank and wants a code from your app. What do you do?
a: Hang up and call the bank yourself
Tell him your PIN as well
128101.e: Banks never ask for codes or passwords on the phone. If in doubt, call the bank's official number yourself.

128102.q: Someone online offers you money if you pass payments on through your account. What is true?
a: It is fraud and you can break the law
It is a good part-time job
It is allowed if you are under 14
Every bank does it this way
128102.e: Anyone who lends their account for other people's money is often helping with money laundering. Such people are called money mules.
128102.m: Your account is only for you.

128103.q: You have won something online but are told to pay a fee first. What is it probably?
128103.e: Real prizes do not ask for payment in advance. Scammers lure people with prizes to get their money.
128103.m: A prize with a fee? Hands off!

128104.q: What should you do if you think you have fallen for scammers?
a: Tell the bank and your parents straight away
128104.e: The sooner the bank knows, the more likely it can stop payments or block cards. Reporting it to the police can help too.
128104.m: Speak up quickly instead of keeping quiet.

128105.q: What is a strong password for online banking?
a: Long, with mixed characters and used only for that
The same as for all your games
128105.e: A long, unique password is hard to guess. If another account is hacked, your online banking stays protected.
128105.m: One account, its own strong password.

128106.q: Which Swiss banknote does NOT exist?
128106.e: Switzerland has notes of 10, 20, 50, 100, 200 and 1000 francs. There is no 500-franc note.

128107.q: In how many national languages is there text on Swiss banknotes?
128107.e: The notes have text in German, French, Italian and Romansh. So all the national languages are included.

128108.q: How do you check whether a banknote is real?
a: Tilt it, feel it and hold it up to the light
128108.e: Real notes have security features that change when you tilt them or become visible against the light. The paper also feels special.

128109.q: What is the smallest coin still in use in Switzerland today?
128109.e: The 1-centime coin was withdrawn in 2007, and the 2-centime coin even earlier. Today 5 centimes is the smallest coin.

128110.e: The 5-centime coin is the only golden yellow Swiss coin. All the other coins are silver-coloured.

128111.q: Which is the biggest Swiss coin?
128111.e: The Fünfliber, the 5-franc coin, is the biggest and most valuable coin. There is no 10-franc coin in normal circulation.
128111.m: The five-franc coin is the king of coins.

128113.e: Coins are made by Swissmint in Bern. The banknotes, on the other hand, are issued by the Swiss National Bank.
128113.m: Coins from Swissmint, notes from the National Bank.

128114.q: What does the abbreviation CHF stand for?
128114.e: CH stands for Confoederatio Helvetica, the Latin name for Switzerland. F stands for franc.

128115.q: Who is shown on the 1- and 2-franc coins?
a: Helvetia, a female figure for Switzerland
128115.e: The standing Helvetia with spear and shield is a symbol of Switzerland. She is on the half-franc, 1-franc and 2-franc coins.

128116.q: Who mainly owns the cantonal banks?
128116.e: Cantonal banks are banks that are wholly or mostly owned by a canton. They are meant to support the economy in the canton.

128117.q: What does the state guarantee that many cantonal banks have mean?
a: The canton is liable for savings if the bank has problems
The bank must give money to all children
The bank may not pay interest
128117.e: With the state guarantee, the canton stands behind the bank's obligations. That gives customers extra security.
128117.m: The canton stands behind its bank.

128118.q: Which company does PostFinance belong to?
128118.e: PostFinance is Swiss Post's financial institution. Many people have an account there for their payments.

128119.q: Can a private person open an account at the Swiss National Bank?
a: No, it is the bank of the state and of the banks
128119.e: The National Bank issues the banknotes and keeps prices stable. It holds accounts for banks and the federal government, not for private people.
128119.m: The National Bank is the banks' bank.

128120.q: Which authority supervises banks in Switzerland?
128120.e: The Swiss Financial Market Supervisory Authority, FINMA, checks whether banks follow the rules. This is meant to protect customers' money.
128120.m: FINMA keeps an eye on the banks.

128121.q: What is the balance on a bank statement?
a: The current amount in the account
128121.e: The balance shows how much money is in the account after all credits and debits. If it is negative, the account is overdrawn.
128121.m: Balance: what is left at the bottom line.

128122.q: Noah had 300 francs. 50 francs are credited to him and he pays out 80 francs. What is his balance?
128122.m: Plus comes in, minus goes out, the balance is what stays.

128123.q: Why should you check your bank statement regularly?
a: To spot wrong or unknown payments
Because otherwise the bank changes its colour
So that the interest goes down
128123.e: If you check your payments, you notice quickly when something is wrong. Report unknown payments to the bank at once.

128124.q: What does a minus sign in front of the balance mean?
a: The statement has been printed wrongly
128124.e: A negative balance means you have spent more than was in the account. The bank usually charges interest for this.
128124.m: Minus means: debt with the bank.

128125.q: What does a bank do with some of the money in savings accounts?
a: It lends it to other customers
It buries it in the garden
It gives it to the canton as a present
128125.e: Banks bring savers and borrowers together. Savers' money is used, for example, for mortgages or loans to businesses.
128125.m: The bank brings savers and borrowers together.

128126.q: What do you normally need to open a bank account?
128126.e: The bank must know who its customers are. That is why it asks for a passport or an identity card.

128127.q: Sara is starting an apprenticeship. What does she mainly need an account for now?
a: So her apprentice's wage can be paid in
So she never gets bills again
So she never needs cash again
128127.e: In Switzerland wages are almost always paid into an account. For this she gives her training company her IBAN.

128128.q: Lena is starting her apprenticeship. Why does her training company need her IBAN?
a: To transfer her wages to her account
128128.e: In Switzerland wages are almost always transferred to an account without cash. For that the employer needs the IBAN. It does not give them access to the account.
128128.m: With an IBAN you can send money, but not withdraw it.

128129.q: What is a salary account (private account) mainly for?
a: An account only for long-term saving
An account for shares and funds
An account only the employer uses
128129.e: Your wages arrive in the private or salary account, and bills, standing orders and card payments go out from it. A separate savings account is better for saving goals.
128129.m: Salary account for everyday life, savings account for later.

128130.q: Why is it worth keeping a salary account and a savings account separate?
a: You can see better what is left for saving
128130.e: If your savings are in their own account, you are less likely to spend them on everyday things. A standing order shortly after payday makes saving automatic.

128131.q: Max gets paid on the 25th. When is the best date for his savings standing order?
a: At the end of the month, if anything is left
128131.e: If you save straight after your wages arrive, you put the money aside before you spend it. What is left at the end of the month is often less than planned.

a: Charges the bank makes for running the account
Interest you receive from the bank
Fines for making too many payments
128132.e: Many banks charge a monthly or yearly fee for the account and cards. For young people and people in training, accounts are often free. It is worth comparing.
128132.m: Comparing fees saves money every year.

128133.q: What happens if you only pay part of your credit card bill?
a: High interest is charged on the rest
The bank pays the rest for you
Nothing happens until the next bill
128133.e: If you only pay part, you are taking out a loan for the rest. The interest on it is much higher than for a mortgage or a savings account.
128133.m: Always pay your credit card bill in full.

128134.q: What does the payment deadline on a credit card statement mean?
a: By then the amount must be paid, without interest
From then on you may use the card again
By then you must return the card
From then on you get a bonus
128134.e: The credit card company sends a statement once a month. If it is paid in full within the payment deadline, there is usually no interest.
128134.m: Meet the deadline and pay no interest.

128135.q: What is the credit limit of a credit card?
a: The highest amount you can spend per billing period
The amount you must spend every month
The balance in your savings account
The number of payments allowed per day
128135.e: The bank decides up to what amount you may pay with the card. Once the limit is reached, further payments are declined until you have paid the bill.
128135.m: The limit is a boundary, not a target.

128136.q: Nina has a credit limit of 2,000 francs. What is true?
a: It is borrowed money that she must pay back
It is 2,000 francs she is given as a gift
It is her wages for the month
The money is already in her account
128136.e: With a credit card, the card company pays first. At the end of the period Nina must pay everything back. A high limit does not mean you can spend that much.
128136.m: Credit card means: buy now, pay later.

128137.q: From what age do you usually get your own credit card in Switzerland?
128137.e: For a real credit card you must be an adult, and the bank checks your income. Younger people can often use a prepaid card or a debit card.

128138.q: How does a prepaid card work?
a: You load money onto it first and then pay with it
You pay everything at once at the end of the month
The bank lends you money every month
You can shop with it without limit
128138.e: With a prepaid card you only spend what you have loaded onto it beforehand. That way you cannot get into debt. It is well suited to young people and travel.

128139.q: What can happen if there is not enough money in the account for a standing order?
a: The bank always pays the amount for free
The recipient gets twice as much
The standing order turns into a savings order
128139.e: Without enough money in the account, the bank often does not carry out the order. Then the bill is not paid and reminder fees may follow. Some banks also charge a fee.
128139.m: Check your balance before the payment date.

128140.q: Why is the overdraft interest rate usually higher than the interest rate on a savings account?
a: The bank takes a bigger risk with a loan
Because saving is supposed to be banned
128140.e: When the bank lends money without security, it could lose it. For this risk it charges high interest. For your savings, on the other hand, it pays little.
128140.m: Borrowing is expensive, saving earns little.

128141.q: What is meant by compound interest?
a: Interest that is also calculated on earlier interest
Interest you have to pay twice
A fee for interest paid late
128141.e: If the interest is not withdrawn, it is added to the capital. The next year the interest is calculated on the larger amount. That way the money grows faster and faster.

128142.q: You invest 1,000 francs at 5% interest. How much do you have after two years with compound interest?
128142.e: After one year it is 1,050 francs. In the second year you get 5% on 1,050 francs, which is 52.50 francs. Together that makes 1,102.50 francs.
128142.m: In the second year, the interest on the interest counts too.

128143.q: What helps most when saving, so that compound interest can work?
a: Starting early and leaving the money for a long time
Withdrawing all the interest every year
Changing account as often as possible
Only starting at the age of 60
128143.e: Compound interest shows its effect over many years. If you start early, you benefit much more, even with small amounts.
128143.m: Time is a saver's best friend.

128144.q: Lia pays 3% interest on a loan of 10,000 francs. How much interest is that per year?
128144.e: 3% of 10,000 francs is 10,000 times 0.03, so 300 francs. This amount is added to the repayment each year.

128145.q: A savings account pays 1% interest and inflation is 2%. What happens to purchasing power?
a: It falls, because prices rise faster
128145.e: The money in the account grows by 1%, but prices by 2%. So in the end you can buy a little less than before.
128145.m: Interest below inflation means less in real terms.

a: Prices rise in general and money loses value
The franc is replaced by the euro
128146.e: With inflation, the same shopping costs more money. So with the same amount you can afford less. The National Bank tries to keep inflation low.

128147.q: How much equity do banks usually require when you buy your own home?
a: At least 20% of the purchase price
At least 2% of the purchase price
At least 80% of the purchase price
128147.e: Banks usually finance at most 80% of the purchase price with a mortgage. You must raise the remaining 20% yourself, at least half of it not from your pension fund.

128148.q: What serves as security for the bank with a mortgage?
128148.e: The mortgage is secured by the property. If the borrower does not pay, the bank can have the property sold.
128148.m: With a mortgage, the house is the guarantee.

128149.q: What does the bank check when assessing whether a mortgage is affordable?
a: Whether housing costs are no more than about a third of income
Whether the house is pretty enough
Whether the house is in a town
128149.e: The bank calculates with a cautious interest rate, running costs and amortisation. These costs should not be more than about a third of gross income.
128149.m: Housing should cost no more than a third.

128150.q: What does amortisation mean with a mortgage?
a: Paying back the debt step by step
The yearly valuation of the house
128150.e: With amortisation you pay back part of the mortgage. This reduces the debt and also the interest costs.

128151.q: What is the main advantage of a fixed-rate mortgage?
a: The interest rate stays the same for the whole term
You never have to pay interest
You can cancel it free of charge at any time
The bank gives you part of the house
128151.e: With a fixed-rate mortgage, the interest is fixed for a certain number of years. This makes planning reliable. If interest rates rise, you benefit; if they fall, you pay more than necessary.
128151.m: Fixed means: same interest, clear planning.

128152.q: What does the interest rate of a SARON mortgage depend on?
a: The current level of interest rates on the money market
The year the property was built
128152.e: SARON is a reference interest rate of the Swiss money market. The mortgage rate adjusts continually, plus a fixed margin for the bank.
128152.m: SARON mortgage: the interest moves with the market.

128153.q: Tim has 150,000 francs in an account at a bank. The bank goes bankrupt. What is covered by deposit protection?
128153.e: Deposit protection covers at most 100,000 francs per customer and bank. For the rest, Tim becomes a creditor in the bankruptcy proceedings.
128153.m: Over 100,000 francs: spread it across several banks.

128154.q: Sara has 80,000 francs each at two different banks. What is true about deposit protection?
a: Only 100,000 francs are protected in total
128154.e: The limit of 100,000 francs applies per customer and per bank. With two different banks, each balance is therefore protected up to this amount.
128154.m: The limit applies to each bank separately.

128155.q: What is NOT protected by deposit protection?
a: Changes in the value of shares
128155.e: Deposit protection protects account balances if a bank goes bankrupt. It does not cover losses from falling share prices. Securities in a custody account, however, still belong to the customer.
128155.m: Price losses are the investor's risk.

128156.q: What happens to shares in a custody account if the bank goes bankrupt?
a: They still belong to the customer and are handed over
They go to the bank's creditors
128156.e: Securities in a custody account are not the bank's money but the customers' property. In a bankruptcy they are separated out and returned to the customers.
128156.m: What is in your custody account belongs to you.

128157.q: What does banking secrecy basically govern?
a: Bank employees may not pass on customer data
Banks may not publish interest rates
Customers may not show their account number
Banks must close all accounts in secret
128157.e: Bank employees are required to keep information about customers to themselves. Anyone who breaks this secrecy commits a criminal offence. There are, however, legal exceptions, for example in criminal proceedings.
128157.m: What the bank knows about you stays with the bank.

128158.q: When must a bank give information despite banking secrecy?
a: When an employer wants to know the account balance
When someone asks on social media
128158.e: Banking secrecy has legal limits. In criminal proceedings, for example for money laundering, banks must give information to the authorities.
128158.m: Banking secrecy does not protect crimes.

128159.q: What are the two check digits after “CH” in an IBAN for?
a: They detect typing mistakes when it is entered
They show the age of the account
128159.e: With the check digits, the system can calculate whether the IBAN is valid. A swapped or wrong character is usually noticed straight away.
128159.m: Check digits protect against typing mistakes.

128160.q: Which information is absolutely necessary for a bank transfer in Switzerland?
128160.e: For a payment you need the recipient's IBAN and name. PINs and passwords are secret and are never needed for payments.
128160.m: For payments: IBAN and name, never passwords.

128161.q: What does the QR code on a QR bill contain?
a: The payment details such as IBAN, amount and reference
128161.e: The Swiss QR Code contains all the details for the payment. You scan it with your banking app, check the details and approve the payment.

128162.q: How can you recognise the Swiss QR Code on a bill?
a: By the Swiss cross in the middle of the code
By a red border around the code
By a picture of the Federal Palace
128162.e: The Swiss QR Code has a small Swiss cross in the middle. That is how it differs from ordinary QR codes.
128162.m: The cross in the middle shows: Swiss payment slip.

128163.q: Paul receives a bill he was not expecting. What does he do before scanning it?
a: He checks whether the bill is genuine and justified
He pays immediately so that no reminder comes
He pays half for now until everything is cleared up
He scans the code and relies on the bank to check it
128163.e: Fraudsters send fake bills too. The bank does not check whether a bill is justified. If you cannot place a bill, check the sender and ask using a number you know.
128163.m: Unknown bill? Check first, then pay.

128164.q: Lena is moving and has a standing order for her old rent. What must she do?
a: Delete or change the standing order herself
Nothing, the bank notices the move
Ask the landlord to send the money back
128164.e: A standing order keeps running until you change or delete it. The bank does not know that the rent is no longer due.
128164.m: Standing orders run until you stop them.

128165.q: What is special about direct debit (LSV)?
a: The recipient takes the amount with your permission
You must make every payment at the counter
The bank gives you the amount as a gift
The amount is brought in cash by post
128165.e: With LSV you give a company permission to take bill amounts directly from your account. This is convenient when amounts vary, for example for electricity.
128165.m: With direct debit, the recipient collects the money.

a: The bill appears in your online banking and you approve it
The bill comes by letter with a stamp
The bank pays all bills without asking
You pay the bill in cash at the counter
128166.e: With eBill, bills come straight into your online banking. You check them and approve or reject them with one click. You can also set up automatic approval.
128166.m: eBill: check and approve bills digitally.

128167.q: What is an advantage of eBill compared with a paper bill?
a: You do not have to type in any payment details
You never have to pay the bill
You earn interest on the bill
128167.e: With eBill, the amount, recipient and reference are already filled in. This saves time and prevents typing mistakes.

128168.q: How can you often recognise a phishing email?
a: It puts you under time pressure and wants you to click a link
It always comes from your best friend
It only asks about the weather
128168.e: Fraudsters threaten, for example, to block your account and demand quick action. The link leads to a fake page where you are supposed to enter your login details.
128168.m: Time pressure and a link: watch out, phishing!

a: Phishing by text message or short message
A secure login with a smartphone
A payment with a mobile phone
A discount on a text message
128169.e: With smishing, fake messages arrive by text, supposedly from Swiss Post or the bank, for example. They contain a link to a scam page.
128169.m: Phishing can come by text message too.

128170.q: You entered your password on a fake bank page. What do you do first?
a: Call the bank immediately on the official number
Wait and see if anything happens
Forward the email and forget about it
128170.e: The sooner the bank is informed, the sooner it can block access and stop payments. Afterwards you change your password and check your account transactions.
128170.m: If in doubt, call the bank straight away.

128171.q: What is the safest way to get into your online banking?
a: Type the address yourself or use the official app
Through a link in an email
Through an advert in a search engine
Through a link in a text message
128171.e: Links in messages and adverts can lead to fake pages. If you type the address yourself or use the official app, you are on the safe side.
128171.m: You choose the way to your bank yourself.

a: A quiz run by the bank
A savings plan with a bonus
128172.e: In quishing, QR codes, for example on letters or parking meters, lead to fake pages. There you are supposed to enter payment or login details.
128172.m: QR codes can be used for fraud too.

128173.q: What is meant by social engineering?
a: People are manipulated to get data or money
A technique to make computers faster
A new kind of bank account
128173.e: Fraudsters exploit trust, helpfulness, fear or time pressure. For example, they pretend to be the bank, the police or technical support.
128173.m: The target is the person, not the computer.

128174.q: A caller says he is from your bank and asks for a code from your app. What do you do?
a: Hang up and call the bank on the number you know
Give him the code straight away
Tell him your password as well
Send the code by text message
128174.e: Real bank staff never ask for passwords or confirmation codes. If you give the code, you often allow the fraudster to make a payment.
128174.m: You never pass on codes, to anyone.

128175.q: Why can a bank's phone number on your display still be fake?
a: Fraudsters can manipulate the number displayed
Because banks are never allowed to call
Because phone numbers change every day
Because only landline numbers are genuine
128175.e: With so-called spoofing, fraudsters make a real number appear on the display. That is why you do not trust the display but call back yourself.

128176.q: Someone offers you money if you pass payments on through your account. What is true?
a: This can be money laundering and is a criminal offence
This is a legal side job
This is a kind of savings account
This is allowed by the bank
128176.e: Such “money mules” help criminals hide money from fraud. Anyone who takes part can commit an offence and is often liable for the damage.
128176.m: Your account is not for hire.

128177.q: What is a typical sign of a scam call?
a: Pressure to act immediately without thinking
You may hang up and call back at any time
The person gives an official number to call back
The person asks nothing of you
128177.e: Fraudsters want to stop you from thinking calmly or asking someone. Time pressure is therefore a clear warning sign.
128177.m: Whoever rushes you wants to trick you.

128178.q: Which factor belongs to the category “something you are”?
128178.e: Biometric features such as a fingerprint or face belong to you as a person. Passwords and PINs are knowledge, the mobile phone is possession.
128178.m: Biometrics: the body as a key.

128179.q: You get a login confirmation on your phone even though you are not logging in. What do you do?
a: Reject it and inform the bank
Confirm it so the message goes away
Switch off the phone and forget it
128179.e: An unexpected request means someone might know your password. Reject it, change your password and inform the bank.
128179.m: Only confirm what you started yourself.

128180.q: What makes a password for online banking secure?
a: It is long, unique and not used anywhere else
It is the same for all accounts
It is on a note stuck to the screen
128180.e: A long, random password is hard to guess. If you only use it for the bank, your account stays safe even if another site is hacked.

a: People with earned income subject to AHV contributions
Only self-employed people with their own company
128181.e: Anyone with income in Switzerland that is subject to AHV contributions can pay in. Apprentices who earn wages count too.

128182.q: What immediate advantage does a payment into pillar 3a bring?
a: It can be deducted from taxable income
You get the amount back twice
You no longer pay health insurance
You may withdraw the money at any time
128182.e: The amount paid in is deducted in the tax return. This lowers income tax in the same year.
128182.m: A pillar 3a payment lowers your tax bill.

128183.q: When is the earliest you can normally withdraw the money from pillar 3a?
a: Five years before the AHV reference age
128183.e: Pillar 3a savings are meant for old age. Normally you can withdraw them at the earliest five years before the AHV reference age. There are a few legal exceptions.
128183.m: Pillar 3a money is tied up for old age.

128184.q: For what may you withdraw pillar 3a money early?
a: For buying a home you will live in yourself
128184.e: Early withdrawal is only allowed in certain cases, for example for your own home, for starting self-employment or when emigrating permanently.
128184.m: Early withdrawal only for important reasons.

128185.q: What is the difference between a pillar 3a account and pillar 3a with securities?
a: With securities there are more opportunities, but also ups and downs
128185.e: A pillar 3a account pays interest without any price risk. With pillar 3a funds the money is invested. In the long run this can bring more, but the value goes up and down.
128185.m: More return means more ups and downs.

128186.q: Why is it often worth starting pillar 3a early?
a: The money has longer to grow
The bank then gives you a present
128186.e: If you pay in early, you benefit for decades from compound interest or investment returns. On top of that comes the tax deduction every year.

128187.q: What do you buy with a share?
a: A small part of a company
A savings account with fixed interest
128187.e: As a shareholder you become a part-owner of a company. You can share in profits, but also bear losses if the price falls.
128187.m: A share means: a piece of a company.

a: A loan to a company or the state that pays interest
A share in the ownership of a company
A credit card with a high limit
128188.e: With a bond you lend money. In return you get regular interest and, at the end of the term, the amount back, as long as the borrower can pay.
128188.m: A bond means: lending money for interest.

128189.q: What is the biggest risk with a bond?
a: That the borrower cannot pay it back
That the interest is too high
That you get too many dividends
128189.e: If the company or the state runs into payment difficulties, you lose part or all of your money. That is why unsafe borrowers pay higher interest.
128189.m: High interest, higher risk of default.

128190.q: Which statement about shares and bonds is true?
a: A share makes you an owner, a bond makes you a lender
A bond makes you an owner
A share always pays a fixed interest rate
128190.e: With a share you have a stake in the company. With a bond you have lent the company money and receive interest.
128190.m: Share: a part. Bond: a loan.

a: A pot in which the money of many investors is invested
A single piggy bank at home
128191.e: Many investors pool their money. Experts or a set rule invest it in many shares or bonds. That way the risk is spread.
128191.m: A fund bundles a lot of money in many securities.

128192.q: What does diversification mean when investing money?
a: Spreading the money across many different investments
Putting everything into a single share
Buying and selling shares every day
128192.e: If you spread widely, you lose less when a single investment does badly. This lowers the risk without giving up opportunities completely.
128192.m: Don't put all your eggs in one basket.

128193.q: Jan puts all his money into the shares of a single company. What is the problem?
a: If the company does badly, he loses a lot
He does not have to pay taxes
128193.e: A single company can get into difficulties. Without spreading his money, Jan takes the full hit. With many securities the damage would be smaller.

128194.q: What is usually the link between risk and return?
a: Higher chances of return mean higher risk
High returns always come without risk
Low risk brings the highest return
128194.e: Investments with big chances of profit go up and down more and can also bring losses. Safe investments, on the other hand, usually bring less return.

128195.q: An offer promises 20% return per year without any risk at all. What do you make of it?
128195.e: High returns without risk do not exist. Promises like this are typical of investment fraud, often on the internet or social media.
128195.m: Too good to be true? Then it usually is.

a: How long you probably will not need the money
How far you live from the bank
How high the interest on your savings account is
128196.e: If you will not need the money for a long time, you can sit out ups and downs of shares more easily. Money for the next few months belongs in an account instead.
128196.m: Short-term money does not belong in shares.

128197.q: What does the volatility of an investment describe?
a: How much its price goes up and down
How high the bank fees are
128197.e: High volatility means big ups and downs in the price. For investors that means more uncertainty about the value at a particular moment.

a: An index of the largest Swiss shares on the stock exchange
A savings account at the National Bank
128198.e: The Swiss Market Index includes the 20 largest and most traded shares on the Swiss stock exchange. It shows how these companies are doing overall.
128198.m: The SMI is the thermometer of the Swiss stock exchange.

128199.q: How high is withholding tax on dividends in Switzerland?
128199.e: Withholding tax of 35% is deducted from dividends and from larger interest earnings. If you declare the earnings in your tax return, you get it back.

128200.q: What is the main task of FINMA?
a: It supervises banks, insurers and financial markets
It sets the key interest rate
128200.e: The Swiss Financial Market Supervisory Authority grants licences and checks whether financial institutions follow the rules. In this way it protects customers.
128200.m: FINMA: the supervisor of the financial centre.

128201.q: A provider in Switzerland accepts customers' money but has no licence. Who can step in?
128201.e: Anyone who accepts deposits from the public on a commercial basis needs a FINMA licence. FINMA can take action against unlicensed providers and warns the public about them.

128202.q: How can you check whether a financial provider in Switzerland is licensed?
a: Look it up on the FINMA website
Ask the provider and believe them
128202.e: FINMA publishes lists of licensed institutions and a warning list of suspicious providers. That is more reliable than advertising.
128202.m: Check with FINMA first, then invest.

128203.q: What is the most important task of the Swiss National Bank (SNB)?
128203.e: The SNB conducts Switzerland's monetary policy. Its main goal is price stability, while taking the development of the economy into account.

128204.q: What does the SNB understand by price stability?
a: Inflation of less than 2% per year
Prices that fall slightly every year
Inflation that exactly matches pay rises
128204.e: The SNB equates price stability with a rise in consumer prices of less than 2% per year. It also wants to avoid deflation, meaning falling prices.

128205.q: Which statement about the SNB and FINMA is true?
a: The SNB makes monetary policy, FINMA supervises the institutions
FINMA sets the key interest rate
128205.e: The SNB steers interest rates and the money supply. FINMA licenses and supervises banks, insurers and other financial institutions.

128206.q: Who receives most of the SNB's profit distributions?
128206.e: If the profit is large enough, the SNB pays part of it out to the public sector. One third goes to the Confederation, two thirds to the cantons.
128206.m: One third Confederation, two thirds cantons.

128207.q: What must a bank check by law before giving a consumer loan in Switzerland?
a: Whether you can pay the loan back
Whether you already have an account with it
128207.e: The Consumer Credit Act requires a creditworthiness check. This is meant to stop people from getting too deep into debt.
128207.m: A loan only if repaying it is affordable.

128208.q: How long can you cancel a consumer credit agreement in Switzerland?
128208.e: Under the Consumer Credit Act you can cancel the agreement in writing within 14 days. That leaves time to think the decision over.
128208.m: Two weeks to think it over with a consumer loan.

128209.q: What can happen if you do not pay bills despite reminders?
a: The creditor can start debt collection proceedings
The debt disappears after a month
128209.e: With debt collection proceedings, a creditor can claim the money through legal channels. An entry in the debt collection register can later make it harder to find a flat, for example.
128209.m: Unpaid bills catch up with you.

128210.q: Why can withdrawing cash with a credit card be expensive?
a: There are usually high fees and interest
Because you get the money twice
Because the card becomes invalid afterwards
128210.e: For cash with a credit card, many providers charge a fee as a percentage of the amount. Interest is often charged from the day of the withdrawal as well.
128210.m: Better to get cash with a debit card.

128211.q: Lea pays by card abroad. The terminal asks: in francs or in euros? What is usually cheaper?
a: In the local currency, so euros
Not paying by card at all
128211.e: If you choose francs, the shop often does the conversion, usually at a worse rate. If you pay in euros, your own bank converts at its rate.
128211.m: Abroad, pay in the local currency.

128212.q: Your bank card has been stolen. What do you do straight away?
a: Have the card blocked using the blocking number or app
Wait and see if the card turns up
Only change the PIN in the app
Go to the bank branch on the next working day
128212.e: The sooner the card is blocked, the less damage can be done. A new PIN is not enough, because contactless payments work without a PIN. Afterwards you report the theft to the police.

128213.q: When do you often have to bear the loss from misuse of your card yourself?
a: If you kept the PIN together with the card
If a hacker attacks the bank
If the card was copied through no fault of yours
If the bank makes a mistake
128213.e: Banks require you to handle your card and PIN carefully. If you write down your PIN and keep it with the card, you are breaking this duty of care.
128213.m: PIN in your head, not in your wallet.

128214.q: What does a Swiss bank always require when you open an account?
a: A letter of recommendation from your school
128214.e: Because of the rules against money laundering, banks must know who their customers are. That is why they check a passport or identity card.

a: Hiding money from crimes so that it looks legal
Making counterfeit money and putting it into circulation
Hiding income from the tax office
128215.e: Criminals try to hide where illegal money comes from. Banks must report suspicious cases to the Money Laundering Reporting Office.
128215.m: Dirty money does not get clean, it gets tracked down.

128216.q: The rule of 72 estimates when money doubles. Roughly how long does it take at 6% interest?
128216.e: You divide 72 by the interest rate: 72 divided by 6 gives 12. At 6% interest with compound interest, money doubles after about 12 years.
128216.m: 72 divided by the interest rate gives the doubling time.

128217.q: What happens on a stock exchange?
a: Securities such as shares are bought and sold
The National Bank issues new banknotes
Banks give mortgages to home buyers
128217.e: On the stock exchange supply meets demand. This creates the price of a share. The Swiss stock exchange is in Zurich.
128217.m: The stock exchange is a marketplace for securities.

128218.q: What is the smallest coin you can pay with in Switzerland today?
128218.e: The smallest coin today is the 5-rappen coin. The 1-rappen coin has not been legal tender for many years.
128218.m: The 5-rappen coin is the smallest coin.

128219.q: Which Swiss coin is also called the “Fünfliber”?
128219.e: The large 5-franc coin is popularly called the “Fünfliber”. It is the largest and most valuable Swiss coin.
128219.m: The Fünfliber is worth five francs.

128220.q: Which Swiss coin is gold in colour?
128220.e: The 5-rappen coin is golden yellow. The other Swiss coins are silver.

128221.q: What is the smallest banknote in Switzerland?
128221.e: The smallest note is the 10-franc note. For 5 francs there is no note, only a coin.
128221.m: The smallest note is the 10-franc note.

128222.q: What is the largest banknote in Switzerland?
128222.e: The largest note is the 1000-franc note. It is purple. There is no 500-franc note in Switzerland.

128223.q: Mia has two 2-franc coins and one 1-franc coin. How much money is that?
128223.e: 2 francs plus 2 francs makes 4 francs. Add 1 more franc, and that makes 5 francs.
128223.m: First add it up, then spend it.

128224.q: How many 20-rappen coins do you need to make one franc?
128224.e: 5 times 20 rappen makes 100 rappen. And 100 rappen is one franc.

128225.q: How many 50-rappen coins are worth the same as a 2-franc coin?
128225.e: Two 50-rappen coins make one franc. So for 2 francs you need four of them.

128226.q: What is written on every Swiss coin?
128226.e: Every coin shows its value, for example “1 Fr.” or “20”. It is also stamped with the year it was made.
128226.m: The number on the coin shows its value.

128227.q: Leo has a 10-franc note. He would rather have coins. What can he do?
